translations.text: Commentary on the Psalms of David
First discourse, a letter of Dachi to the blessed Stephen, bishop of Mtbevari. Venerable father, holy bishop Stephen, chosen one of Christ, my lord!
Blessed is God, who has revealed you as a good shepherd for us and as a spiritual physician who builds us up.
Many times I have desired to see you, for the healing of the pains of my soul, but because of the distance and the cares that leave me no leisure, I have not been counted worthy to pay you reverence.
Now may I be forgiven for this, that I am sending you by letter this work of mine for your judgment, holy one of God.
For a long time I diligently sought the commentary on the Psalms, the book written by our holy father Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus,
and I did not find it in Georgian. I found it in the Greek language, but I could not understand it; it was like an inaccessible spring and a hidden treasure.
Then I found it written in the Armenian language, complete, with the same Greek arrangement and the same numbering.
I felt zeal on account of the Armenians, yet I was afraid to translate, for great guilt befalls translators who are not careful.
And indeed, if someone has already translated a work in full, a second translation appears as opposed to the first, as with those of Aquila and Symmachus, and for this reason it is not fitting.
But I did not find it previously translated, and therefore I have translated this small portion as a tasting and have sent it before your God-loving self for judgment.
So judge it according to the wisdom that has been given to you, and if it is fitting, let these be planted in the church by you. But if this book is of no worth,
burn it and conceal my rashness, and reprove me, and I will repent. Out of those hundred and fifty readings I have brought out only seven,
that is, only the recitations [?] in full, and without your command I will undertake nothing further, until I know whether I would have any reward if I were to labor,
or whether I would labor in vain and guilt would befall me. For the commentary on those hundred and fifty psalms is a great book, the psalms which David, the pen of God, wrote.

By the Holy Spirit he composed a prize of praise and placed it on the crown of the head of the church, for victory over the enemy. The commentary of this our holy father Epiphanius shows us everything well and in good order:
what those superscriptions are, or how it mentions Asaph and the sons of Korah and Jeduthun and the other singers, or when and for what reason the psalms were spoken, or what
meaning "of the winepresses" and "inscription on a pillar" have. He shows us every single thing, so that not even one iota remains that he does not explain well to us.
Just as the holy apostles dined with the Lord on the shore of the lake of Tiberias with a hundred and fifty-three fish, in the same way the holy patriarch
Epiphanius prepares those fish and gives a meal to all the faithful. For those books of the Psalms are bread and divine grace in the holy church.
But I, according to my ability, have sent you these few out of those hundred and fifty [?].
If it is fitting that the work be completed, let your holiness complete it. I, because of my lack of leisure, am able to do nothing.
If anything is not fitting, as was mentioned above, burn it and grant me forgiveness, and may I be remembered in your prayers, venerable father. Amen.
Psalm 1: "Blessed is the man who has not gone to the counsel of the ungodly."
The marvelous and blessed prophet and great king David, how he cries out all at once and calls by inspiration to the only-begotten
Son of God, and since, or insofar as, by prophecy he is made like his Lord and Creator Jesus
Christ, who went up and sat upon the mountain, when he wished to send out the apostles to preach blessedness to the world by his teaching.
He makes blessedness the beginning, and starts to speak: "Blessed are those who are weary in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."
He spoke of what belongs to the Spirit, of how it is possible to be mingled with God and akin to the Spirit.
And David calls blessed and purifies the renewal of the spirit, that is, in counsel: "Blessed is the man who has not gone to the counsel of the ungodly."
O song mingled with the Spirit and adorned with blessedness, which the prophet David sings and psalms, speaking thus:
"Blessed is the man who has not gone to the counsel of the ungodly, and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of the lawless."
This must be examined carefully, O beloved: whenever those who translated the divine books find a superscription in the Hebrew, they translate the superscription as well, after the same manner.
But for the first psalm, and the second that comes after it, they found no superscription, nor did they translate anything additional;
they only wrote it down, with souls seized by fear, and did not dare to write anything added to the words of the Holy Spirit.
Now let us state the meaning of the psalm, for certain people, rashly, who cannot attain to the meaning of the psalm, have said
that "this psalm is spoken about one matter only, and not about the order of the law," and again they rashly took it upon themselves, on their own authority, to compose
and write a superscription; they wrote the meaning of the psalm as one thing and another, and spoke in various ways, and for that rashness of theirs I place them among the heretics.
But I know this with discernment: that I find the meaning of the psalm to be rather about the order of the law, and together with it, as one matter, for it speaks about the lawless and the ungodly.
This is what it has said about the order of the law, and then together with it about the judgment and destruction of sinners.
Now come, let us begin to explain and let us speak at this time: "Blessed is the man who has not gone to the counsel of the ungodly."
He calls blessed only those who have not shared in the lawless, disorderly and ungodly counsel of the gentiles,
and who have not gone to the deed and way of sinners, and have never stood to be with them and to hear their words,
for they do not stand and wait on the way in order to share with them; this is what he says: "He has not stood in the way of sinners."
Rather, he fled from the counsel and dwelling of the ungodly, the lawless and the sinners.
He confessed and believed in the only God and the blessed only King of kings.
The witness is the God-bearing apostle Paul, who cries out, saying: "of the blessed and only mighty King of kings and Lord of lords,"
[?] who has granted us grace and made human beings sharers in the glory of his divinity, for he says thus:
"God is faithful, by whom we were called into the communion of his Son."
God says to the blessed Moses: "He is faithful to me, and there is no guile in him."
And he calls people "faithful to me": the faithful, who do not hold his words lawlessly or double-heartedly,
those called faithful of God, co-heirs of the only-begotten Son of God, whom he named gods.
With such a gift may people walk forever. With a loud voice David sings and cries out and says: "I said:
'You are indeed gods, or sons of the Most High, all of you; you shall die like men, and like one of the princes we shall fall.'"
David speaks rightly and calls blessed the one who with courage was able to reach the end and brings forth the fruit of righteousness,
just as each person courageously brings his own craft to completion with knowledge, for then he is to be called blessed:
when the physician drives away the multitude of diseases and brings the sick person back to health, and when the strong man wins the victory by felling a valiant opponent.
And so everything else, each in its own way, is brought to completion in goodness by the working of righteousness, when people receive the blessedness of God for themselves.
We also see another force in the word of blessedness, as though blessedness belonged only to males. It says, "Blessed is the man."
Christ does not speak his blessedness only for the male, nor only for the woman, nor does he exclude the goodness of women who are fruitful;
rather, this word of blessedness unites the head with all the members, for "the head of the wife is the husband, just as we are all the body of Christ and our head is Christ."
All we members have received salvation and life, and we have set the crown of grace on our head, Christ;
likewise here it says, "Blessed is the man": it unites the head with the body and crowns the head.
Let all his members rejoice, for the members are not separated from the head.
So too it says, "Blessed is the man": together with him it has also called blessed the holiness of women.
See, blessedness separates us from their counsel and way and dwelling, so that we may not sit in the seat of the lawless.
Now let us speak of them together, for it was not idly that first came the counsel, and next the ways, and then the dwellings; but let us look at this carefully.
If before the stirring of words we have freely examined [?] whether something is good or evil, then,
after this, we may join their dwellings and firmly and resolutely come to sit down together with them.
See, blessedness warns us and teaches us here as follows: do not accept the counsels of ungodliness in your mind, and do not habitually wait on the way to share with sinners,
nor sit with them in the seat, for such seats are the heads of evil and perdition, of pagans and the lawless.
Scripture lovingly gives this commandment to those who keep themselves from such things; but those who are deniers and godless, and who worship many gods,
and who are partners in counsel and partners in service with them, these are utterly lawless and pagans.
But he classes as sinners those who commit adultery with their blood relatives, lawfully [?], and do filthy things, and through defilement lawlessly corrupt their own souls and bodies,
who not only defile their own souls with sin, but also become a cause of sin for others and lawlessly corrupt them, and by sodomy
and by bestial lust corrupt their own souls and bodies with lawless deeds of filth.
He does not command us to sit with such a lawless person in his seat.
That is, not to join in their deeds. Rather, flee from their lawless deed and practice holiness completely, for it says this: "Turn away from evil, do good."
And again blessed Isaiah cries out and says: "Cease from your evil, learn the practice of good."
In the same way David sings psalms and chants, and he removes us from the counsel of the lawless, from the walk and dwellings of sinners, and from the seat and the rule of the lawless.
And with joy, of our own free will, he leads us to the law of the Lord, speaking thus: "But his will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he meditates day and night."
He speaks not only of this one precaution, to keep far from the lawless, the sinners and the ungodly,
but also of being, with joy in the divine law, always united with it night and day and speaking it, with one's will being with it,
which the divine law has commanded us, as the law commands your rule [?] of deeds of ascetic striving in accordance with uprightness,
for the God of all, for the sake of the upright, lays down the law upon us by the hand of Moses and says this:
"Let the words of this law be in your mouth at all times, to meditate on it, both at your rising up and as you walk on the way.
And let them be bound to your hand at all times, and let them be immovable before your eyes."
And here he shows us a beautiful tree watered by the water of the law, well-rooted and clothed, planted to bear fruit,
whose fruit is renewed at all times and fills everyone, for the psalmist sings thus and says:
"He shall be like a tree planted beside the streams of water, which will yield its fruit in its season.
And its leaf will not fall. And whatever he does will prosper for him," for the divine Spirit waters like water,

and by grace makes spring up, as if in the likeness of water, a tree planted beside the channels, clothed in leaves and well-rooted, so as to fill with fruit such hearers [?] of the words of the deed [?].
He who has prepared himself by divine deeds and brings forth divine fruit,
such is the joy through the water of the only-begotten Son of God. And Christ, the Lord of all, gave the name of water to his own teaching:
"You who thirst," he says, "come to me and drink," and "the water that I will give him will become for him a spring of living water, and it will lead him to eternal life."
And again: "Whoever believes in me, as the scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly."
Again the Lord says to the Samaritan woman: "Whoever drinks of this water will thirst again.
But whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again."
Thus again he says through the hand of Isaiah the prophet: "I will give water to the thirsty and to those who walk in the waterless land."
"And I will make water spring up on the mountains, and rivers shall flow on the hills, and I will give drink to the people whom I have chosen,
and to the congregation that I have made as my inheritance." Now, in keeping with this figure, blessed David, who through devoted leisure came to maturity in the divine Scriptures,
gave the name of a tree planted and bearing fruit beside the channels of water,
for those who, by purity and righteousness, with their own wholly adorned struggle and by bringing forth their fruit,
whose leaf, the leaf of their good things, is by their hope always green and rooted.
And they exult with joy, and in hope they show love to their soul, at all times gathering heavy labors,
for he has close beside him a helper and the great gift of his Lord. This, with all eagerness, he has made to prosper well for his righteous ones.
"And for those who love God," says the divine Paul the apostle, "all things prosper well."
For this reason blessed David says: "Everything whatever he does shall prosper for him," for the Lord is the prospering of their walking and of their ways, and they desire them greatly.
Now all this they did not write in vain, but they confirmed it with great reverence; and first, all evil and sin
he commanded to be abandoned and willingly put far away, and then one is to submit to one's own God and to do what is perfect, for he says thus:
"Everything whatever he does shall prosper for him," for we know that nothing is opposed to the divine law.
And those who take up the words and the law of God, let them desire it of their own free will, for he says, "In the law of the Lord is his will, in his law."

Thus is accomplished the work of righteousness: to act with courage and to attain the perfection of knowledge, to become lovers of truth and philosophers, and so to lead oneself onward with wisdom and easily to find, and to conquer by truth.
Now let us speak of what befalls those who are wholly ungodly and are not like them. "Not so the ungodly, and not so."
He says the word twice, and of the most extreme and evil torment for them: "but like the dust that the wind scatters from the face of the earth."
But the righteous, he says, shall be watered by the words of the divine books, as by the water of life, and shall be beautifully green at all times,
and, mingled with flowers, shall bring forth their fruit; but sinners, on the contrary, are at all times lost and vanished and unstable,
like the dust of the earth, trampled down by every evil thought of their soul.
"Therefore the ungodly shall not rise up at the judgment, nor sinners in the counsel of the righteous."
With great exactness he has reverently shown us about the resurrection of soul and body altogether, and about the judgment.
He did not say, "Sinners shall not rise," but he says, "They shall not rise for judgment," for they shall rise not to be judged but to be condemned,
for no conviction is needed for them, nor any judgment to come upon them, whose conviction is this very thing, that of the deeds of their ungodliness,
but punishment and torment stand prepared and await them, as they do grave-robbers and murderers;

They do not bring them to the place of judgment in order to convict and condemn them, but inflict torment on them according to the law; in this manner the lawless and the godless will be given over to torment at the resurrection.
No one keeps them for judgment, but they receive punishment very quickly, as do those who are evil in mind and the heretics who speak improperly of the mystery.
Such people do not join in the counsel of the orthodox, for they seized and split the law and went outside the law.
In the same way they have departed and have not joined the assembly and the counsel of the righteous, for Aquila and Theodotion translated "counsel of the righteous" as "assembly of the righteous."
Symmachus joined his wording to theirs as well. Now let us speak in due order: "For the Lord knows, it says, the way of the righteous, and the way of the ungodly will perish."
He knows, it says: the one who knows all things knows everything, for nothing is hidden from him, and before his coming to judge he knows the just judgment.
And he has no need of any testimony or any conviction, but renders to each person what is deserved according to his own deeds:
he crowns his valiant and holy ones, but sinners he does not bring to judgment; rather, he sends them away to punishment in the eternal fire.
At that time the way of the ungodly will perish, in keeping with the deeds of their walking, and the word of the apostle will be fulfilled, that "in whatever deeds they were,
they will receive their reward according to their deeds, and some to the resurrection of judgment, for torment; that is, they will live immortally, but they will live in this way, as from fire,"
for the resurrection of the righteous will flash brilliantly like light, in accordance with their deeds, but the ungodly at the resurrection will perish, yoked together with their evil deeds.
Psalm 2: "Why have the nations been stirred up, and the people devised vain things? The kings of the earth conspired, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his anointed."

In the first psalm he mentioned the lawless at the end, at the end of the psalm, but in the second psalm he mentions the lawless first, and he shows us their error, how they were maddened together with one another,
which the kings and rulers and Jews and gentiles plotted and carried out against the Savior.
For the second psalm is about the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ;
it prophesies concerning his sufferings in the flesh, his kingship, and the faith of the gentiles toward him, and it laments the ungodliness of the Jews;
for his word is, "Why have the nations been stirred up," and how greatly he shows us the guilt of the people and the exposure of their foolishness.
And there is no need for our inquiry to explain this, any difficult word in the psalm,
for the divine leader, the apostle Peter, explained it in the Acts of the Apostles and said thus:
"Herod and Pontius Pilate, the chief priests and scribes, the kings and rulers gathered together for the crucifixion of our Lord Jesus Christ."
For Pilate had been sent from Rome, and Herod held the rule over the Jews.
Many other Jews and gentiles, who vainly plotted against the Lord to hand him over to death, did so in futility, because
after three days he rose and received worship from all the ends of the earth, and the commandment of the holy Gospel testifies to this:
"Then the chief priests went out and took counsel as to how they might destroy him."
At that time Caiaphas said: "It is better for us that one man should die, and not that the whole nation should perish."
As for the passage that says, "Why were they stirred up?", Aquila says, "Why did they [?]," while Symmachus said: "Why were they thrown into confusion and turned aside?"
And as for the passage that says "the Gentiles": for the Jews seized Jesus and were leading him away, and they were saying: "He is an opponent of Caesar."

It was as though he desired kingship, and as though by tyranny he were an evil opponent [?], that they accused him before the Greeks, for they were killing him, and they laid on him a charge deserving death.
And they led him outside, to the place of the skull, to destroy him. And as the blessed Luke says, they accused him and said:
"We found this man, who was speaking to everyone and forbidding them to pay tribute to Caesar, and who called himself Christ and king."
"Let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke away from us."
After this he came with the company of the saints, and those arrayed in order, who are believers together, say:
Let us burst the [?] of the Gentiles and cast away from us the yoke of the lawlessness of the Jews, and let us take up the sweet yoke of Christ, for these are his words:
"Take up my yoke, for my yoke is sweet and my burden small and light." For the God-clothed Peter calls the Law a yoke,
when he says in the Acts of the Apostles: "You are testing God by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples,
which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear; but through the grace of God, of our Lord Jesus Christ, we believe that we have salvation."
Now behold, David, with prophetic eye, by the grace of the Spirit, speaks beforehand the word of what he saw.
"Let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke away from us.
Let him who dwells in the heavens laugh at them, and let the Lord treat them with contempt." For some of them nailed him and gave him over to death by the cross.
But he himself was and is in all places in fullness, and he receives glory from the ministers of heaven.
Now behold, he looked upon those doers of vanity, and he who dwells in the heavens laughs at them and treats them with contempt, and with a cry he says to those defeated ones:
"I was set up as king by him." And they brought [?]; thus it says: "on Zion, his holy mountain."
Not on Zion alone did he become king, but king over all created things, visible and invisible.
For this reason it says Zion, because the beginning of the kingship of the Jews was from Zion; all believed the ordinance and command of the King from Zion.
To this the saying bears witness in which he says: "Go and make disciples of all the nations, and baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit."
At that time he says, "I was set up as king by him," for it is as a man that he says, "I was set up as king"; but he himself, as he is God, possesses dominion and kingship.

Rather, he says "I was set up as king" of his own labor, for everything that he did in service to us was for our benefit; but he himself is God, timeless and without beginning, mighty in his own kingship.
The prophet bears witness with a cry and says: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, the rod of your governance and the rod of your reign."
For at all times you are most high and you dwell among the high places. David cries out in song and says: "You alone are most high over all the earth."
He speaks of his labor and of his divinity, for thus Zechariah says to John: "Now you, child, will be called prophet of the Most High."
You, the very same one Son, who is equal to the Father, were born today from the virgin Mother of God in our nature.
And the Son himself accomplished by labor, in his own flesh, everything that was needful.
This he has taken up, as from the mouth of the Son, and the blessed David cries out with a great voice and says: "The Lord said to me: 'You are my Son, and today I have begotten
you.'" At that time no one is able to understand this except through the teaching of the Holy Spirit: he says "Son" with reference to the divinity, in the words "You are my Son,"
and with reference to the bodily birth from the Mother of God, "today I have begotten you."
Therefore come, and let us hear the word of God Almighty, who says by the mouth of David: "From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you."
Now behold, the true Son of God has stature, for in his flesh he heard all this, and to him the whole world has been entrusted, and he leads us to the glory of God.
And he asked for us for redemption, and for all the Gentiles as his inheritance, for he says thus:
"Ask of me, and I will give you the Gentiles as your inheritance, and all the ends of the earth for you to possess," for the true Creator of all is worthy,
for all things came to be through him, and without him not one thing came to be, and he created all things visible and invisible, and he is the Maker and Creator of all.
Although he is Lord and God, he took up, as a man, the labor for all the ends of the earth, for at that time they were reviling in this way,
saying that the Jews alone are the inheritance and people of God, because the Lord's portion was his people Jacob,
and Israel the lot of his inheritance. But now, after this, he has cast off and removed the congregation of the Jews from his inheritance, because
he found nothing better among them, for they had become fighters against God; justly he transferred his inheritance to the Gentiles.
And he had understood this beforehand, and he instructs them and proclaims the joy of the Gentiles and says: "Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people!"
We find this to be a proclamation concerning the Gentiles, for whom the Jews became leaders and whom they called to the inheritance, and the Gentiles rejoice with them over the gifts of God.
Not only the twelve tribes of the Jews, but also the seventy disciples and more than five hundred brethren,
to whom he appeared after the resurrection, and the God-clad Paul, and the assemblies of three thousand and five thousand, to whom Peter, the head of the apostles, spoke in the streets, and who said:
"God-fearing men and many myriads, of whom the great James says: Do you see how many myriads of believing Jews there are?
All this multitude of believing Jews, with whom the Gentiles rejoice";
the word of Moses has been filled and fulfilled, in which he says: "Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people."
The Lord of all filled and fulfilled this and showed us that there is no distinction for anyone who desires the faith, whether he be Jew or Gentile,
for he says thus: "There are other sheep also, who are not of this fold;
They too are worthy to be gathered and brought to me, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one [?] flock and one shepherd."
Before this he prophesies in a psalm; David sings in praise and says: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance."
Now let the Jews show me all this and tell me: who else was it who took possession of all the ends of the earth, whether from among the Jews or from among the gentiles,
if not he alone who sprang up from the root of David according to the flesh, who is our Lord Jesus Christ himself?
Truly the word of the prophet, which he spoke beforehand concerning them, has blinded them all:
They groped for the wall like the blind and the sorrowful who have no guide; having gone astray, they fell into the depths of their punishment.
This the prophet proclaims, saying: "He shall shepherd them," he who was crucified by them, "with a rod of iron."
That is the kingdom of the Romans, for it is the kingdom of the Romans that he calls iron, because it is strong.
Daniel likewise speaks in a parable and calls their kingdom iron. "And like potters' vessels I will shatter them," he says.
God passed a just judgment by the hand of the Romans upon the race of the Jews, for they themselves, of their own accord, cried out and said:
"We have no king but Caesar." So he gave them into the hands of Caesar, whom they sought, who by his might shepherded their iniquity with a rod of iron.
If they do not say this of this passage, upon whom would this saying be fulfilled, except only upon those from whom he took the city and laid it waste?
Now after this the prophet turns his speech from the assembly of the Jews to believing kings and says:
"Now, O kings, understand this, and be instructed, all you judges of the earth."
Look at the Jews, whom he taught as with a rod of iron; learn from them, and flee from those false Jews.
"Accept instruction, lest the Lord be angry," for he is our King, "and serve the Lord with fear and sing to him with trembling."
Now it is fitting for all to serve the Lord and to sing to him with trembling, out of dread of his torments, and not merely to rely on God's love for humankind,
but with fear and trembling, out of dread of his torments; and along with goodness let one hasten to practice holiness and rejoice over his salvation.
Along with joy there must be fear and trembling, for it says thus: "Whatever will or nature has given you, beware of it, lest it cast you down."
"Accept instruction, lest the Lord be angry and you perish from the right way," for it is not only great knowledge of God and faith that lead to perfection,
but together with faith there must be works of holiness, by which one may firmly lay hold of everything.
Then after this, the one who has been filled will attain perfection in his own time,
"when his wrath suddenly flares up," and those swift torments surround them on all four sides, and they are burned like firewood, consumed by fire.
But those who find comfort, the worshippers of God and doers of justice, who hoped in the mercy of God,
have taken up the labors of their work and received the crown of glory and become blessed, for the prophet says thus:
"When his wrath blazes up, blessed are all who hope in him." What is this that he says?
Those who live by evil deeds are prepared for torment by fire, but those who live by deeds of righteousness, God has made blessed and crowned.

Psalm 3. A psalm of David, when he fled from the presence of Absalom his son. The narrative and the meaning of the psalm are clear, and the twofold rashness and wickedness of Absalom are greatly and exceedingly astonishing.
And still more, and to a greater degree, the meekness and righteousness of David are astonishing, how he was able to endure trials of many kinds,
for not only did the neighbouring Gentiles rise up to make war against him, but other evil and lawless wraths were also sent upon him within his own house.
What shall we say of the eagerness for his father's death of Absalom, the slayer of his brother, who went further still and rushed to carry out persecution even against his father,
so that by the grace of the Spirit David, through his courage, was delivered from all of it and even more found victory?
But at this time, behold, because of the multiplying of his adversaries and because of the many and various trials coming upon him, he cries out to God and says:
"Lord, why have my oppressors multiplied? And many have risen up against me.
Many say to my soul: 'There is no salvation for you from God.'"
Many, and very harshly, were driving many to despair, saying that he will not find deliverance from God.
But I truly and firmly know that you will not turn your face to pass by those who call upon you, even if they are full of many sins.
And now with much fervour I entreat you because of the bitter evils and unjust persecutions that I have gathered from my son.
Exalt me and strengthen me all the more over my pursuer and his fellow counsellor, for this is what he shows us by his words:
"You, Lord, are my helper, my glory and the lifter of my head," for at this time I do not trust in my kingship and my power, but with faith I await help and glory from you.
And you are the hope to which I entrust myself; swiftly raise up my right hand: "With my voice I cried out to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain."
For he says this: with all the desire of my mind I offer prayer before you, for I know that you fill up and fulfil for each and every person their requests.
And it is not a voice and sighing and crying of that outward kind that we must understand here,
but rather asking help from God with great spiritual desire and fervour and wordless sighing, for this is the very thing that the God of all says to blessed Moses:
"Why do you cry out to me?" And by "crying out" he means that wordless prayer which takes place in the heart and mind.
And "he heard me from his holy mountain": it found fulfilment according to the custom of the voice [?], for they supposed thus,
that the testimony of the God of all is only at the Tent of Testimony, for only from there did the high priests receive the everlasting answer to their inquiry.
"I lay down, I slept, I awoke, for the Lord became my helper."
The books have many times called night and sleep distress and affliction and the attack of the godless, for in darkness there is truly night without light,
the going of his dwellings and counsels [?]; but the sign of night is the attack of the godless, and sleep is the affliction that has come upon one.
And because of that affliction he prays and asks for salvation to be brought about, and he says: "I awoke, and the Lord became my helper," for this reason:
because I found God's help greater than all my enemies; they were frightened and struck with terror, but I escaped without fear from the many who had risen up against me.
Therefore he says: "I was not afraid of the myriads of people who surrounded and encompassed me round about."
Your salvation has become great and abundant upon me by your will alone. All my enemies have fallen and been crushed because of this, by the will of God, he says.
"Arise, Lord, save me, my God, for you have struck down all who were my enemies without cause; you have broken the teeth of sinners."
Now, behold, truly strengthen me and bring your salvation to completion upon me,
as you have done at all times, according to your custom of delivering me from my many oppressors, both from foreigners and from Israelites, both from strangers and from those of my own household,
whether from Amalek and from the assembly of the Assyrians, or from Saul my king, who brought injustice upon me and wished to snatch me away, as a lion would.
You struck his jaw with a bridle and delivered me from his midst.
Now show your power to be great and surpassing, for you have heard my entreaty and, according to your custom, have broken the teeth of sinners.

Now even more be for me a house of refuge and save me. This is what he means when he says, "You have broken the teeth of sinners": the mighty who have come up against me and the multitude of soldiers,
those murderers. Deliverance is from the Lord, for it is not a man, but you, my Savior, and your salvation, O Lord,
that I await; and not I alone, but also this assembly, which, united with me, is persecuted by that assembly of those who have fought against me.
When they see our deliverance, they will turn and come to serve, and I shall be king over them, and may peace be upon all!
And I beseech your mercy, O Lord my God: bring about salvation and peace for this assembly, and grant the blessing that is from you,
for thus he announces to us and says: "From the Lord is life, and your blessing is upon your people."
For in all the books he commands the high priests to bless the people with peace,
when they go out to battle, or when they return, or at the festivals of their year and of the assembly.
Then all the more does David take up song, and with psalms he blesses and asks mercy and peace for his enemies and persecutors,
for it was the Holy Spirit who spoke through him, by whom he desired the salvation of every person and their being brought to the knowledge of the truth.
David is a type of Christ, and Absalom is a type of the Jews, the persecutors of Christ.
Psalm 4. Of the end, a song of David with crying aloud. In place of saying "of the end," Aquila and Theodotion indicate to us "for the making of victory"; Symmachus said "for victory."
Thus they indicated to us, by saying "of the end," that after long and many times and at the end of days he will hate [?] the prophecy.
At the end of the psalm he instructs us beforehand and says: "In peace I will lie down upon it and sleep, for you, Lord, alone have made me dwell in hope."
He speaks of the victory that came about for blessed David, which preceded the psalm, concerning Absalom, his son.
Therefore you [?] from this psalm this psalm, for [?] of all, for his request was heard.
They spoke a song of victory, to the effect that "there is no salvation for him from his God."
But with this psalm: "Sons of men, how long will you be hard-hearted? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?
Understand that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful," he shows us by this psalm those who are godless and cannot understand the mercy of God,
who is able to deliver from every affliction, and nothing is impossible with him, for his power is made perfect in weakness.
For this psalm was spoken as a reproof for the lawless and the godless: "When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me."
He says: See and believe how this salvation came about for me, and how it all came down upon me in word and in deed.
And God, in power and openly, quickly heard my crying out, for I sent my prayers to him and he heard my request.
And as for his saying, "By my righteousness alone," he means this:
by my request for righteousness, and not that David here testifies in pride to his own righteousness and courage,
for God says concerning these same words, by the hand of Isaiah the prophet:
"Then you will call me and I will hear you," and before your calling to you I said, "Here I am." "In my affliction give me relief, O Lord!"
It is the custom of all first to send a little affliction upon his saints, and after this to scourge them,
as we have seen, through the struggle of their torments, in order to recount everything, also concerning their witness, as with Job and Abraham,
on account of trials, for while they were still in trials, he would strengthen their souls and make them victorious over their enemies.
For this reason David now cries out with a loud voice and sings and says:
"Now behold, from affliction and weakness and lowliness you have strengthened my soul and helped me, and from narrowness you have made me broad."
And this is what God's love for humankind says, the God-bearing Paul:
"My grace is great for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." He looked upon me and heard my prayer.
The God-loving soul will not be silent, but at all times it has the custom of praying, in spaciousness and in narrowness, and it brings forth its fruit as a sacrifice,
that is, works of righteousness; and it cries out to God unwearyingly and by song reproves the hard-hearted and says:
"Sons of men, how long will you be hard-hearted, why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?" Receive from me and understand and learn,
sons of men, God with great love for humankind and mercy. And those who call on him with heart and mind, he will quickly hear them;
Now cast away from you the thought of vanity, and "understand that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful; the Lord has heard me, my crying out to him."
For it was not in some idle or slight way that he came to his aid, but openly he delivered him many times from death and established him as victor and ruler over all his enemies.
For this reason he says: "Understand that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful."
Here again he calls "holy" the faithful and sinless, meaning that no fault lay with those whom they were persecuting.
He calls "wicked and hard-hearted" the unbelievers, who had seen such great salvation from God and yet shamelessly came against the righteous, heavy of heart,
like someone who is inflamed with wine and goes mad, weighed down and dizzy, and he [?] and rolls about, and vapors rise up from his head, by which
his mind is seized, and his hands are numbed, his eyes heavy and closed like those of a dead man, and he can hardly look up.
In just the same way are the unbelievers and the wicked. For this reason he has today raised the voice of crying out and says: "In your anger do not sin,"
at the time when you act and are enraged, do not oppress anyone and do not repay anyone evil for evil.
If it is not right to repay evil for evil, why do you repay evil for good?
"What you say in your hearts, repent of upon your beds," for by "bed" he means calm, and night, the time of rest.
For then thoughts are without turmoil, whereas by day nature draws to itself every assault.
But the lawgiver teaches them and says to them: "Offer to the Lord a sacrifice of righteousness and hope in the Lord."
We have examined and found this in the commandments of the old law and in the incense offerings and sacrifices of Moses,
for Gentiles and Jews used to offer incense, just as heretics and Gentiles now make incense offerings.
But this is the will of God, of which he says: "Offer a sacrifice of righteousness and hope in the Lord."
In the same way our Lord Jesus Christ says to his disciples: "I am the vine and you are the branches, and my Father is the vinedresser;
every branch that is planted in me and does not bring forth fruit, my Father will cast it out."
He did not say this idly, but said, "that is planted in me."
That is to say, whoever is not so by my command, in the way that I have given the faith and the law;
there are many who do not strive toward the faith and the knowledge of God, and who seek glory from men.
For this reason he also shows us, and wishes for justification through courage of various kinds. "Many say: Who will show us the good of the Lord?"
He says this about those upon whom sorrow and affliction at some time come, and who despair of themselves and, wearied by faintheartedness, say:
"Who will show us the good of the Lord?" Now behold, the good of God distinguishes us, one from another, from those who have become hasty.
But we say: "The light of your face has appeared to us, O Lord.
"You have given joy to our hearts": for they were deliberating in dejection and speaking in human fashion because of their own unbelief.
But those who came to be through the knowledge of God that comes from you [say]: "We have believed in you, and the light of your face has appeared to us,"
that is, the faith of the knowledge of Christ, "and those who had risen up against us and were afflicting us have perished together, well, and you have given joy to our hearts."
And again he is indignant at those ungrateful ones and says to them: God's benefaction is with them: "He has filled them from the fruit of their wheat and wine and oil."
And again he rebukes the same people who say, "Who will show us the good things of the Lord?"
How can one who has received so many benefactions of the Lord say, "Who will show us the good things of the Lord?" — those who rejoiced, filled from the fruit, with their wheat, wine and oil.
He rebukes those who have received the good things of the earth and do not know how to give thanks to God.
For by these three he shows us all the good things of the earth; and in hope they received all this good, and yet in their haste they dared to say, "Who will show us the good things of the Lord?"
But I say: Receive the good of our Lord and the hope of the knowledge of God; I believe, and in that peace, by this hope, "I lay down and fell asleep.
And I awoke, for you, Lord, alone have made me dwell in hope."
All those who were shaken and became unbelieving and turned to the earth by the thought [?] of their own — deliver such as these, O God,
by your mercy and benefaction; become their guide to hope and make known to them peace and the hope of the resurrection, for death has seized them in the manner of sleep;
for just as someone awakens from sleep, so likewise, and even more so, we await repose and resurrection from death.
Here he shows death as sleep for those who rest without fear in the hope of the resurrection.
For there are some who, because of their evil deeds, are terrified of death and have become despairing of the resurrection.
But David boldly sets forth the pledge of hope, and reckons death as sleep, and joyfully proclaims the awakening with hope, and with a loud cry believes in the joy of the resurrection.
Psalm 5 of David, for the end, concerning the heir. All those who have explained and interpreted the superscription have made clear in it why, to the Word of God,
that is, his only-begotten Son, he joined his Church and called it heir; for its head is Christ and its members are these, each one individually his own,
who in the service of God walk toward life in the purity of their conduct; for the Lord says concerning such people in his honored Gospel:
"Come, you blessed of my Father, and inherit the kingdom prepared from the beginning of the world."
And the chosen servant of God Paul says: "The Spirit of God bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God.
And if children, then also heirs with God and fellow heirs with Christ."
And again: "We are not a slave but a child; and if a child, then also an heir through Christ."
Now concerning inheritance we find many other things as well in the divine books.
This is the force and nature of the psalm, for as far as we have come in close detail to enter upon the words of the psalm.
"Hear my words, O Lord, and understand my cry; attend to the voice of my prayer."
Many times and from many sides trials and storms have arisen and come upon the Church, and not only upon one church, but upon all souls
who are named with holiness. Afflictions and terrors were sent upon them, but the Church and her saints have gained victory over all her enemies.
Even though trials were stirred up to fall upon the rock, the gates of hell do not prevail against it.
But all this happened so that our courage might be shown all the more and that we might offer our supplications to God,
just as the teaching now instructs us how it is fitting for all to offer supplication and sighs to God and King.
It teaches us thus: "Hear my words, O Lord, and understand my cry; attend to the voice of my prayer, my King and my God."
Now, it is not that he perceives a cry through crying aloud, for it is not that he has ears attached for hearing,
for whatever bodily things the Scriptures say about God are for our instruction and not on account of the nature of the Godhead.
Now, whatever bodily sorrow they speak of, it comes about in the manner of their limbs,
just as Elijah, with great boldness, had zeal for God, he who said thus: "The Lord lives, before whom I stand today."
"For you, O Lord, are not such as to desire lawlessness; the wicked shall not dwell before you, nor shall the lawless stand before your eyes."
Hear my request and remove terrors from me; I know the afflictions of ungodliness,
for all the ways of walking and the deeds of disorder are foul before you; and let those who come not walk their ways in ungodliness.
David has taken this up as a song, and he says openly in his psalm:
"You have hated all who work lawlessness; you will destroy those who speak falsehood; the bloodthirsty and deceitful man the Lord abhors."
The deeds of wickedness, and of those who desired to oppose God, and their deeds of contention were abhorred and cast away more than just once.
But although they brought many afflictions upon the saints, they could not overcome them; rather, they themselves, by their own doing, perished instead far off [?],
for although from time to time they became zealous, they still could not come against and oppose the word of our Lord God Jesus Christ, for he says:
"The gates of hell shall not prevail against it." In this same psalm he says this openly:
"But I, by your great mercy, shall enter your house; I shall worship toward your holy temple in fear of you."
Those who say: Deliver me from all trials, and with your right hand shelter me from all the trials that have been sent, which are named,
that is, "the gates of hell"; and because at all times we offer worship in the temple of your glory,
for I cannot forget the love for mankind by which you have graciously granted me boldness.
"O Lord, lead me in your righteousness, and because of my enemies make your way straight before me," for at all times your ways are inscribed before my eyes.
I see this from each one of them, for he speaks of the way of the upright, and again of their being guarded all the more by God.
Now then, if because of my deeds you cover me with the shelter of your wings, and lead me and direct me, then order my ways.
Symmachus said: "Make straight and direct my way, O Lord." Isaiah also testifies to this and says: "The difficult shall become a plain, and the rugged a straight way."
And again in another place David says: "The walking of the upright is from the Lord, and he greatly desires his ways."
The words of the elders [?] are full of great humility; those who beseech God concerning their enemies are promised a dwelling place,
where there will be no war. They ask for a right, straight and easy way, and to one another they openly recount and denounce the blasphemy of the ungodly,
and their lawlessness and their foul words. Therefore he says: "There is no truth in their mouth;
with falsehood they defile themselves at all times with their tongue; their heart is made vain," for at all times they devise empty schemes, and full of iniquities are
their mind and their mouth. "Their flesh is opened like a tomb," for closed tombs are shut up with the stench of their odor,
but opened tombs often send up that odor of their stench.
In the same way, with fornication, with every defilement and stench, they speak and devise words of blasphemy with their mouth;
that is, their lawless thoughts and their blaspheming tongue, they who at all times insolently send forth their tongue against God and against his saints.
He says: "With their tongues they deal deceitfully," for their thoughts are full of all guile and crookedness.
These are more wicked than those who silently, by themselves, deal deceitfully in secret.
If they open their mouth, they send forth stench and the breath of blasphemy against God; and if they are silent, they speak deceit.
"Judge them, O God; let them fall from their schemes; for the great mass of their ungodliness cast them away." And may he bring them to judgment, and may they be condemned.
Let them rise to be tried for their deeds, they who wove them like a spider's web.
Let them fall through the vanity of their schemes; and at the resurrection they are worthy of punishment for their insolence.
For this reason he says: "For they have embittered you, O Lord," for in their insolence they wished to make war even as far as you.
Now show your power and cut off their insolence, and gladden those who hope in you, for behold, this psalm speaks thus:
"Let all who hope in you rejoice in you forever; let them delight, and you shall dwell among them."
Those believers who hoped in you were filled with joy and received eternal delight.
Those departed, and these were settled. "Let all who love your name boast in you, for you have blessed the righteous."
By the blessing that comes from you and by your mercy he found rest and relief from his afflictions; he boasts in you and speaks in accordance with that word of Paul:
"Let him who boasts boast in the Lord." "O Lord, you have crowned us as with a weapon of good pleasure."
The holy books call "good pleasure" their good and divine will, by which he has strengthened us, as he has protected his saints as with a shield. For in another place it says:
"Lord, you have taken pleasure in your land." This is said to mean: you have willed good for the inheritance of those who fear you.

Now here it says this: by the good pleasure and goodness of your will, and by the abundant love for humankind that your mercy shows toward us, be for us a shield of refuge, for complete victory over all our enemies by the victory of your power.
Place on our heads the crown of joy. This is what it means when it says: "As with the shield of your good pleasure you have crowned us."

Psalm 6. With cries, a psalm of David, for the end, a song concerning the eighth. It draws near to the eighth, and the prophetic word then ordains that there will be three hundred [?] days of rest and of the kingdom,
for the times which willingly [?] move within those seven days of the Sabbath.
For it begins from the first day and goes up to the seventh, and from there it begins to act again as at the beginning, and takes up once more, from the first day, those seven courses.
And this is greater than those seven days, outside those times, that is, above the whole world. This it calls the eighth day.
This psalm mentions the day of resurrection and of the kingdom, in connection with death and hell and judgment, for it speaks thus:
"There is no one in death who remembers you, or who in hell will confess you."
It shows us in this way that the doors of repentance will be shut. Once people have departed from here and gone there, there is no repentance for anyone
who, here in the passing life of this world, proved unable to take up repentance.
There, there is no confession for repentance before God. This statement is witnessed to by the parable he told about the virgins,
for through them it was made clear to us: those who were foolish virgins, whose lamps had gone out [?], and who remained outside the doors of the wedding feast,
the doors were shut and the curtain drawn, and once the doors are shut no one is any longer permitted to enter inside.
Now come, after this let us first begin to take up the words of the psalm and say:
"Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath." It is not this that I beg of you, "do not rebuke me"; rather it says, "do not rebuke me in wrath."
Nor do I beg this of you, "do not discipline me," but rather, "do not strike me in wrath." Instead, like a merciful father,

discipline me with your mercy and compassion, and with gentleness teach me the blotting out and healing of my sins. Do not torment me with eternal torment, and do not repay me with judgments according to my sins,
but teach me with your love for humankind and your justice. It says: "Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak."
Truly, whenever they grow weak because of thoughts, the reasoning powers of our souls become sick;
through that ruling part of our mind our souls are overcome. After this we sin by the thought of the soul.
And if we had not grown weak, disease could not have been with us. For just as charioteers,
who with great training and management want the [?] of their horses, and they are directed straight, so that after this nothing wicked or going crookedly is found among them any longer.
"Heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled, and my soul is greatly troubled."
Here he brings forward the twofold nature and the two matters, showing us that the soul and the body receive what is good together.
For he speaks of the trembling of the soul as complete, with all its strength and with bone and flesh.
But by your love for humankind relieve me and heal me from the anguish and the evil pains of my sins. "And you, O Lord, how long?
Turn, O Lord, deliver my soul, save me by your mercy."
He says "how long," not as though he were accusing or reproaching in any way, but as if to say: out of great affliction and anguish, send help quickly and relieve me, O Lord.

I beseech you. For this reason he brings this forward and says "for the sake of your great mercy," for I do not trust in my own strength, and how by your love for humankind should I have dared to speak before you,
for I have grown weak and have fallen because of heavy sins; but I entreat your great mercy and ask it of you.
"Turn, O Lord, deliver my soul." That is: look upon me and have mercy on me, and do not turn your face away from me.
He says, "and never remove your mercy from me," for I know
that it is here that there is repentance and remission of sins, and that after this life the doors of repentance and remission are shut; for he makes this clear by these words,
that "there is no one in death who remembers you, or who in hell will confess you."
Therefore, while I am still in this passing life of this world, I beseech you and ask of you healing and blotting out: grant this to me and forgive my sins.
I know that for those who have departed from here and gone there with wounds and many sins, there is no healing of wounds there,
nor do they find remission of sins, for there is no place of repentance there for the remission of sins.
"I have grown weary with my sighing; every day I wash my bed; with my tears I drench my couch."
I know that great evils pass away through sighing and tears and much fervent asking,
my mind being like fire, and because, on account of temptations, the countenance of my soul is sorrowful to the point of trembling.
And he brings this forward and says: "My eye has been troubled with anger," for in the sight of my mind I am confused and have fallen away from you because of this, my Lord.
Here he calls the mind an eye, for here it is one and not many: "eye" and not "eyes."
"I have been worn out among all my enemies"; or rather, all my enemies have taken vengeance on me and have worn me out and consumed me.
The evils of my sins have overtaken my soul. "Depart from me, all you workers of lawlessness,
for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping, and the Lord has accepted my supplication." Grant me, O Lord, forgiveness and release from my sins.
Now then, stand away from me, you lawless deeds and sins of mine, who are adversaries and enemies to me.

"Be ashamed": for this reason he brings this forward and speaks thus: "Let all my enemies be ashamed and confounded; let them turn back, let them be greatly ashamed, and let them quickly be troubled."
All this being known, all who were hostile to me and by nature brought on sin through their own wickedness fell silent.
And full of falsehood, troubled and enraged in their heart because they had stripped off righteousness, full of fear, they are terror-struck at the judgment of God.
Psalm 9. Interpretation of "I will confess you": "For the end, concerning the mystery of the children, a psalm of David." Symmachus: "For victory, concerning the death of the sons,"
and Aquila: "With a blow [?], for victory, concerning the youth of the sons," and Theodotion: "Concerning the tender children." All were in agreement on this and made mention of sons.
This shows us the word of prophecy, that this psalm is spoken concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, who conquered by his death,
who, as a chosen man and a mighty youth, conquered the tyranny of sins and gave death not a single cause to find in him,
and he destroyed its dominion and power. As for what it says, "concerning the mystery," this is the hidden counsel that the Son of God carried out.
The seventy translators said this, which it says. This is its explanation: that it was not manifest and known to all.
And why do I say "to all," when it was what he told and taught many times to the apostles alone?
The whole matter that Christ accomplished by deliberate counsel was unknown and hidden.
And the evangelist testifies to this, for the Lord told the disciples many times:
"Now behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of the lawless, and they will crucify him and kill him, and on the third day he will rise."
The evangelist brings this forward in this way and says: "And it was hidden from them, and they did not know what he was telling them," concerning which Paul cries out and says:
"We speak the wisdom of God and the hidden counsel, which none of the rulers of this world knew; for if they had known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory."
And again: the hidden eternal counsel he revealed by generation to his sons.
After this let me look at the arrangement and the sense of the psalm. Come now, and let us approach the words of the psalm to consider them together:
"I will confess you, Lord, with all my heart, and I will recount all your wonders; let us rejoice and be glad in you, and let me sing to your name [?], Most High."
He has laid his whole heart and mind, perfected in itself, before God, and with thanksgiving all the good tidings
that he has wrought he has taken up to sing, and with thanksgiving he recounts them to us and shows us his love of the service of God.
And it is for this reason that it says: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength,"
and it did not command us the deliberation of our love of silver together with love of God, and love of gold together with love of Christ, of this world and of the one to come.
Whoever thus divides his thought here and there cannot, with his whole nature, entirely in unity, say: "I will confess you, Lord, with all my heart."
But the prophet, with the eyes of those of tempered heart, purifies all his inner and hidden thought, and with the eye he sees the hidden mind beforehand [?].
Not only does he say just once, "I will confess you, Lord, with all my heart," but he recounts all his wonders and sets all of this straight for us,
Which I have heard, not by the glory and power and health of the body, but by deeds of purity, by beauty and spiritual grace.
Let us praise and glorify God; let us rejoice and be glad in you.
And similarly to this he says somewhere else: "I remembered God and rejoiced," and again: "Rejoice and be glad in the Lord, you righteous," and again:
"The hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice," for: "Let all my enemies be turned back; let them grow weak and perish from before your face."
These [words] of mine [?] Symmachus translated thus: "Let me sing to your name, O Most High; let all my enemies be turned back; let those who have gone astray perish from before your face."
This is what he says: "I shall see my enemies and oppressors destroyed, fled far away, and all the blows come upon them."
All this saying of the prophet concerns human nature, through which the rule of the evil one was struck down and our mind was saved from slavery.
He brought [us] to freedom and destroyed the ungodly one, the tyrant far from God; by his power he graciously granted us deliverance and life,
as a king the only-begotten Son of God sat upon the throne and renders recompense with the scales of judgment;
by the fall of the enemies he delivers us from the hands of our oppressors, for which reason he has raised up a song; he sings psalms and hymns and says:
"You have carried out my judgment and my justice for me," in a certain manner.
And he says: "You sat on the throne of righteousness; you rebuked the nations, and the ungodly one perished; you blotted out their names forever and ever and ever."
Nor after this is the enemy now able at all to look upon our life, to seize human nature for death, and bitterly to enslave it by tyranny.
Rather, human nature has seen [him], as one seated on lofty thrones and awesomely, as a judge, and [the enemy] himself, as an evildoer,
judged and struck by him, that is, as by a king, and blotted out and destroyed forever and ever, by force [?], and the rule of the devil [likewise].
At that time he says: "You rebuked the nations, and the ungodly one perished." This reveals the deed of the apostles,
which the nations did to Barnabas and Paul in their error and ignorance; but they rebuked their ungodliness and said to them: "What are you doing?
For we are men just like you; but turn from your ungodliness and serve God."
And again Paul rebuked the Galatians: "O foolish Galatians, who has envied you, you who before your own eyes saw the Lord Jesus Christ crucified?"
This is what he says: "You rebuked the nations, and the ungodly one perished; by name you blotted [them] out forever and ever and ever."
They became lawless [?] and until they were entirely filled with their own wickedness.

But now they have thus been removed and have perished through evil forever, as though it had never at any time been joined to the thoughts of any people, and as though the service of idol worship had never existed.
"The sword of the enemy has failed utterly, and the cities have been laid waste." For he was stripped, from that face [?], of the weaponry of ungodliness,
for he found no one to help his lawlessness, those who with wisdom and craft produced [objects] of evil worship and many images.
Behold, the cities have been laid waste, which had been built with strength and great labor,
Their places were destroyed and laid waste, and "their memorial perished" from the earth; the grace of the only-begotten Son of God appeared.
This is what the God-receiving Paul said: "For the grace of God has appeared as savior to all people, teaching us,
that we should renounce ungodliness and the desire of the world, and live with sobriety and righteousness and godliness in this age."
This is the renunciation of all ungodliness, and from the baptismal font let us become crucified together with Christ, as the God-receiving Paul says:
"If we share together in his death, so shall we also be in the resurrection; and again, if we die with him, we shall also live with him."
And thus he destroyed the harsh city of lawlessness and ungodliness, and built upon the rock and established the church and city of godliness.
"Their memorial perished with a cry, and God abides and is forever."
He says plainly that amid ungodliness he takes away the service of lawlessness and the service of God [?];
forever and ever the almighty power abides, and his kingship will never pass away.
"He has prepared his throne; he himself will judge the world with righteousness, and the people and the congregation with uprightness."

Not only in this world has he shown us his might, but for that coming, future world as well he has shown people the judgment that is terrible to all, and each person will receive a reward according to his deeds.

"May the Lord be a refuge for the fallen, a helper in good time, just at the time of tribulation." For "just at the time," Aquila rendered "time" as "season" [?], and Symmachus as "the time that has arrived."
And when he speaks of the poor as fallen, he means human nature, because those who had fallen into much ungodliness and tribulation perished in the time of tribulation.
Paul proclaims and says: "When we were children, we were hated and enslaved to the created things of this world; when the end of the times came,
God sent his Son, who came and was born of a woman and came under the law, so that those who were under the law might be redeemed and received as sons."
"Let all who know your name hope in you, for you do not forsake those who seek you." Aquila and Symmachus translated "let them hope" as taking refuge;
this declares such a deliverance as we have received from you: we have come to know you as Creator and God, and we hope in you and take refuge in you.
"Sing to the Lord who dwells in Zion." Although in the Old [Testament] he speaks of the glory of Zion,
afterward he foretells the prophecy concerning the daughter [?], which we have learned from the God-receiving Paul.
We have drawn near to the heavenly song, to Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. "Declare his deeds among the nations."
For "deeds," Symmachus said "wisdom" and Aquila "change." Truly a great change came about from the work of power:
enemies became beloved, and they were separated [?]; those who were near and slaves became sons, and those who were ignorant became knowing.
And those who were in darkness were enlightened, and those who were in death were made alive by hope, and the poor became heirs of the kingdom of heaven.
The Jews were removed far off and the gentiles came near; sons became dogs and dogs became sons.
All these things came about by the wisdom of the Savior, in a manner befitting God.
He granted them immortality in place of their death, and they passed through death to life, from reviling to glory, from curse to blessing, and by the cross to redemption.
All of this is the wonder-working of the only-begotten Son of God, who changed all these things, for "in seeking vengeance for their blood he remembered, and he did not forget the cry of the fallen."
Whoever has seen all this and has searched out the truth has exposed the eager haste of the devil,
who was eager to destroy every human being. And He did not disregard this, but came and drew near to us and took vengeance on the tyrant.
For this reason he indicates with this saying that "he did not forget the cry of the fallen."
Here by "cry" he does not mean some prayer and petition; rather, those who through their own sin had fallen into diseases, afflictions and deaths were all lamenting:
"Have mercy on me, O God, and see my humiliation at the hands of my enemies." That is, those on whose account we became poor.
And they lamented with tears: Now we ask life of you, so that we may be able to be delivered from the gates of death,
"you who lift me up from the gates of death, so that I may recount all your wonders."

This is what he calls the fulfillment of his goodness, when he delivered us from corruption and dissolved the power of death, at every time and always your blessing "in the gates of the daughter of Zion!
And we shall rejoice in your salvation." He called the heavenly city Jerusalem "Zion," as blessed Paul taught us,
and he called the church, the house of God, which is found throughout all the earth, the gate of the heavenly city, because the church leads us to the heavenly city,
which belongs to the faithful. On account of all this he says at this time: Delight yourselves, and sing in ordered ranks. Lord Jesus Christ, give rest to the soul of Dachi.
Interpretation of the exposition of Psalm 44: For the end, concerning the change of the times, of the sons of Korah, of wisdom,
a psalm for the beloved. Before this psalm the prophet uttered many words in sorrow and told them to us, but by this psalm he has granted us joy and a gift.
He has taken up praise and sings with laudation; he shows us this with delight and gladdens every soul, and he bestows and grants victory to all his righteous ones,
and God's help not only against those of the flesh alone, but he also sets the very head of all ungodliness, the devil, to be crushed, and makes him to be trampled underfoot.
For by the coming of the only-begotten beloved Son of God in the flesh from the root of Jesse, he also brings about the change and renewal of all the gentiles and of their forms of worship,
as the superscription above said: "for the beloved." He called the only-begotten Son of God "beloved," for thus Isaiah prophesies and says:
"I planted a vineyard in a beloved vineyard-place, in a firm place, on a fertile horn."
This one the Father sent down from heaven with a greatly audible voice, and he explained Isaiah's word to us and said: "This is my beloved Son; listen to him."
This only-begotten and beloved Son of God, through holy baptism and the font, by change grants renewal to all the gentiles, and by the Holy Spirit all become sons of God.

For this reason too this psalm sings with praise and says, commanding them to forget the false gods of their fathers and to know the true God, and it changes them from godlessness to righteousness and fruitfulness, and to flourishing in the work of holiness.

For this reason Symmachus translated "change" as "flourishing," while Theodotion and Aquila translated it as "lilies," for the lily flower springs up strongly on the mountains and beautifully opens its petals and blooms.
They are watered by the Spirit of water, through the only-begotten Son of God, as Isaiah said:
"Let the trees of the desert rejoice, and let the glory of Lebanon be given to them, and let them bloom like lilies," for he shows us the beloved Son of God as planter and laborer.
Those who were unfruitful in the desert he changed into bearers of fruit.
This is the sense and force of the psalm concerning the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God.
Come now, let us proceed to the explanation of the words of the psalm: "My heart has uttered a good word."
The Father uttered the only-begotten Son. The Word uttered by the Father came forth as Savior of the whole world; "and I will tell my works to the king."
He whom the superscription called beloved, here he names king.
"My works," he says: he gave this name to his prophetic ministries, for David was enlightened by the grace of the Spirit.
He has raised up praise, and with song he reveals the Word of the Father to all, and he names that king the beloved Son of God.
He continues thus and says: "My tongue is like the pen of a skillful scribe," for it is not that I say or prophesy anything of myself, nor do I conceive it in my mind and devise it,
but by the grace of the Spirit my tongue is made like a pen;
seized by the Holy Spirit and joined to him, it stands within the divinely composed commandment and writes this in diverse ways, beautifully and beyond all scribes.
He named his tongue a pen; he himself possesses it by the grace of the Holy Spirit, surpassing that of all scribes, and whatever he wishes, he writes with it.
Now I shall begin the very great and surpassing prophecies, namely: "He is beautiful to behold, more than all the sons of men; grace has been poured out from your lips;
therefore God has blessed you forever." God has blessed you.
You whom the Father called Word, I name king and son, for your goodness and all your beauty and honor,
surpassing all the sons of men. Grace was poured out from his lips for this reason: that by the hand of his fleshly tongue, as from a spring,
he made all teaching and wisdom spring up. He blessed forever for this reason: that through him all the races of men were redeemed and blessed.
"Gird your sword upon your loins, O mighty one, in your beauty and your goodness; bend your bow, go forward and reign."

The sword is girded on your loins with might, for this reason: that the only-begotten Son of God opposed godlessness and humbled and destroyed it, and with his good teaching he filled the whole world and made it flourish.
This is your beauty and goodness, bent [?], prospering, and he reigns, for he made the opposing powers to be trampled underfoot, he brings about uprightness and rules as king.
He continues in like manner and soon says: "For the sake of truth and peace and righteousness":
Rightly and beautifully the prophet says this openly, calling him the only-begotten Son of God, in truth and humility and righteousness and kingship and lordship.
The explanation of this is not at all difficult for us, for the Lord himself said openly in the Gospel:
"Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls," and again: "I am the way and the truth and the life."
And again he says to John, the bearer of the Spirit: "Permit it now, for thus it is fitting to fulfill all righteousness."
For this reason also he destroyed the sorceries and tyrannies of the devil, did away with death, and granted redemption and life to those who believe in him.
"Your right hand shall guide you wondrously," it says; for on this account he mentions the sword earlier here, and here he rightly gives it the name "right hand,"
for with his right hand he brings punishment upon the lawless for their insincere counsel, as Paul says: "Upon every ungodly and disorderly person you extend [?] the sword."
And these are the punishments: "Your arrows are sharpened, O mighty one, and the peoples fall beneath you, and in the heart are the enemies of the king."
He calls the chief priests and the Jews the enemy of the king, those who said to the Lord's face:
"We have no king but Caesar," by whose arrow, that of the Caesar of the Romans, they fell; and the city and temple of the Jews were laid waste and wiped out by the hand of the Romans,
but the only-begotten Son of God himself reigns over all the world and is seated at the right hand of God,
for whom at this time the prophet has taken up a hymn of praise and sings with laudation, saying:
"O God, your throne is forever and ever, the rod of your governance and the rod of your kingdom,"
for much was said concerning the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God and concerning human nature, such as: "He is beautiful to behold, more than the sons of men;
and God has blessed you forever, and grace has been poured out from your lips."
Concerning the union of the natures of God he says: "Your throne, O God, is forever and ever."
Symmachus translates it thus: "Your throne, O God, which is before all ages."
Now behold, he shows us his righteous judgment: "The rod of governance and the rod of your kingdom.
You loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the ointment of joy more than your companions."
He calls him brother and son and companion on account of the incarnation of the Word of God. And "God, your God, has anointed you" is said to his Son,
the only-begotten Son of God, for he truly became man in our nature, took everything upon himself, fulfilled it, and redeemed us.
Likewise here, "God, your God, has anointed you" is said to his only-begotten Son;
he gave him the name God, for the Father anoints with the ointment of the Holy Spirit and the Son is anointed. This is what he means when he says: "God has anointed you,
your God, more than your companions," for we are children of God by grace, but he is the Son of God by nature.
"Myrrh, stacte, and cassia from your adornment and from the temples of ivory, by which they have gladdened you. The daughters of the king are in your honor."
He gives the Church the name of one variously, delightfully and beautifully adorned, gloriously clothed in a garment decked with ornaments, she whom he called his bride and his body.
And he named himself the bridegroom, for he gave the veil the name of his member and his body.
And now he speaks of the suffering of his body as myrrh; on account of the sufferings of death he speaks of stacte and cassia,
which the Magi offered to him when they came, because by his death he bestowed myriads of joys on the whole world.
"From ivory palaces, by which they gladdened you," for kings and rulers, all of them adorned,

openly offer him their service. "The daughters of the king in honor, for they have become worthy": all the women and daughters of the king [have become worthy] as a bride, by which the only-begotten Son of God was called bridegroom.
The daughters of men offer service: this is the Church itself, who are the body of the only-begotten Son of God.
"You have set the queen at your right hand, clothed in a golden garment, adorned and clothed beautifully in many colors."
By the grace of the Holy Spirit the only-begotten Son of God redeemed his Church and made her his queen and bride, and he himself became the bridegroom,
and he took her up and seated her at the right hand of his Father. This is what it says: "And you have set the queen at your right hand."
"Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear: forget your people and your father's house." He called her daughter, for he had seen beforehand with the prophetic eye,
[that] by the grace of the Spirit he himself made her and gave her spiritual birth from above out of the baptismal font which the Church has received, that is, she who is human nature;
she herself became the God-bearer and, with our nature and our flesh, gave birth to the only-begotten Son of God, and now by the font the Holy Spirit has granted us to be children of God,
who has shown us to be children, and he called his own nature his daughter, and says: "Hear, daughter, and see: forget completely your people, your father's house."
It says this concerning the Gentiles, for it speaks of the ancestral land, the worship and the godless people, and of separation from idols: "Cast them away and forget them."
And when you are purified by birth from above and become his daughter, at that time "your beauty will please the king." By great and manifold [?] he here reveals the image of the new [?],
