the indissoluble union of divinity and humanity in himself, of which the prophet spoke by the grace of the Spirit: behold, he appoints the Son as king, ruler and lord.
"The beauty will please" him who purified and set free his Church and united her to his body, "for he himself is your king.
And you shall worship him, and the daughter of Tyre too shall worship him."
Now after this, for he himself became the head of us all, and we his members, by the grace of the Spirit.
But the only-begotten Son of God, in his own flesh, receives worship and sacrifice among us, for he himself is our Lord and we shall worship him.
For this reason too it says: "With gifts the rich of the people shall serve his face."
Here, incidentally, the only-begotten Son of God called the Church his body, which he united to his own body.
And he is Lord, King, Redeemer and Savior, and he is worshipped by all things visible and invisible.
"All the glory of the king's daughter is within; she is adorned and clothed with golden fringes."
Here he called the Church queenship and nobility and enlightener, for this reason: that the only-begotten Son of God himself, in his own flesh, is that very one
who by our nature is given the name of head, and by his grace he made all of us his members.
Now, how by the grace of the Holy Spirit the holy members are distributed, which is this very Church, as Paul says:
"Distributions are given to each person by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and he has [?].
From the Spirit, to some is given the word of wisdom, and to others knowledge from the same Spirit, and to some faith from the same Spirit,
and to others the grace of healings, and to some prophecy, and to some the interpretation of other tongues,"
for he filled people with many graces, and they came into union and became the body of Christ and the Church of the living God.
Fittingly he says, "And all the glory of the king's daughter," and she was given the name "adorned with fringes woven of gold."
This is the very distribution of the grace of the Spirit to each person, for the fringe and the adornment each have their own distinct place,
and again there is unity, for they are joined in one garment, just as their beauty is held together from the roots.
"Virgins shall be brought to the king, and after them her companions; they shall be brought to him with joy and singing, and they shall lead them into the king's palaces."
All became of one accord, and he caused his assembly to be brought in as the Church.
Now these are the virgins, the first and great ones and the leaders, and their companions, who through them were joined in one accord to the Church, which he takes up and explains well.
And he says: "In place of fathers your children came to be; appoint them as rulers over all the earth."
In place of the fathers and in place of the high priests of the Jewish people, their sons became apostles and rulers, not only over Judea alone, but in all the earth they call them rulers,
for this reason: that after their death they became rulers and commanders over sea and land, and they waged war against idols and against sin and its ruler,
between death and the devil, and they destroyed them, and all submitted to the King and our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore "let us remember your name in every generation and generation; therefore peoples shall confess you forever and to the ages of ages."
David, the God-speaking, had seen this with prophetic eye, and he says:
When it comes to pass that your name is remembered, not just one people, but "offspring of offspring," he says, "and generations of generations" will magnify you, O Lord.

For this reason also they shall confess you for all your wonder-working: how you saved the Church and made her a body for yourself, and a bride and noblewoman and queen, and you became her bridegroom and head.
And all believers became a body for you. For this reason also we bless you ceaselessly, not only at one time, but forever and to the ages of ages.
This is what he says: "Therefore peoples shall confess you forever and to the ages of ages."
Psalm 45. For the end, of the sons of Korah, concerning the mystery: the prophet foresaw it many ages beforehand by the grace of the Holy Spirit.
He has taken up praise and sings about the things that were to happen at the end of times, for thus the superscription says: "For the end."
That is, it is a foretelling of what happened at the end of times: how many trials arose against the church, and how help from God reached it from heaven and became its guard.
And as for those who were fighting against the church, he himself made his own flesh [?] and by submission made peace; at that time he called the enemies of the church to be the church.
For the chief shepherd of their gathering made one flock and one congregation. This is preserved as the sense and force of the psalm.
Certain other interpreters did not examine this well, supposing that this psalm is spoken about Gog and Magog, and others, about Ahaz and Pekah, king of the Assyrians.
Now come, let us approach the word of the psalm, and let it show us clearly that it is not spoken only about this,
but about the church and the calming of its trials, for the superscription reads thus:
"For the mysteries"; that is, it shows all of us openly the hidden counsel of the church.
"God is our refuge, strength, helper in the afflictions that have greatly found us."
The psalm speaks of God in just the same way as the one that came before it, which speaks about the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God and about the gentiles,
how they abandoned their ancestral worship and became the church and the body of Christ and sons of God by birth from above, and queen and bride of the King of heaven.
And he made these very apostles his own sons and brothers, rulers in all the earth.
In accordance with that word of the gospel, this psalm recounts how many very great trials came upon the church, and that the company of believers had hope in God.
They stood [?] amid many [?], amid waves, they looked and said: "God is our refuge, strength, helper in the afflictions that have greatly found us."
Behold, they found God as a refuge, like a firm wall, a mighty tower, and they say:
"Therefore I will not fear the trembling of the earth and the shifting of the mountains and the heart of the sea."
Concerning these mountains and valleys Isaiah prophesies beforehand, saying:
"Every valley shall be filled up, and the mountains and hills shall be brought low; the difficult ground shall become a plain, and the rugged ground a straight road."
And by depth and valley he meant the poor and despised nations, who were lifted up to the knowledge of God.
The prophecy has come and been fulfilled, which said: "And every valley shall be filled up, but the mountains and hills shall be brought low:

the heights of the demons and their worship of falsehood, which were upon the high mountains, were also brought low, and the unseen error was taken away from the midst, and the way became right and straight."
"Therefore," for every soul is calm and untroubled: neither at the quaking of the earth, nor at the shifting of the mountains and in the midst of the sea,
that is, he removed the powers of the devil from human beings and sank the nature of the beasts in the abyss of the seas.
This he has taken up as a song, he sings the psalm and says: "Therefore we will not fear the quaking of the earth, the shifting of the mountains, and the heart of the sea."
If it is fitting, by those former exalted ones who were sunk [?] he means the demons and their worship.
Now the depth of the abyss has utterly swallowed them up, and they are not to be seen. "Their waters roared and were troubled; the mountains were troubled by his might."
The Acts of the Apostles teach us how the company of the apostles turned the turmoil of all the ends of the earth into peace, at Ephesus in the matter of Demetrius,
who, like a mountain, had been raised up for the service of demons and stirred up the city in wrath against the apostles. And the same thing happened at Lystra and Derbe.
And again in the city of the Philippians, and at Thessalonica, Athens and Corinth, there was the maddened, foul spirit of the demons, made into a mountain, raised up.
All these waves and agitations rose up against the holy apostles, but the apostles, like horses harnessed to the chariots of God, set their course over many waters.
The blessed Habakkuk prophesied this, saying: "Your steeds will go upon the sea, to trouble and stir up the waters of the abysses."
He called the company of the holy apostles horses and steeds, who are harnessed to the divine chariots; those who have become sons of God he calls a chariot.
Thus: "You mounted your chariots, and your cavalry is salvation."
Your bow came forth, that is, the preaching and gospel of the apostles and their ministry, and the loftiness of the demons [?], for the destruction of their error and from the defiling spirit,
which, like the thoughts of turbid and storm-tossed water [?], and it made all souls pure and cleansed them.
And they dried up and came to know the true God. This demonic thing he calls a torrent: "Their waters roared and were troubled; the mountains were troubled by his might,"

for the turmoil and tumult of the loftiness of the demons has fallen away from us, and it has become a straight and direct way for all, for "the course of the rivers and of the holy waters gladdens the city of God."
Here he called the gospel a river, and the church a city, along with those who are given life by it through the service of God,
and the course is those who are watered with faith by the divine gospel and become fruitful.
The three translators expressed this more beautifully: first, they say, "the course of the rivers gladdens the city of God";
just as they divided the spring that rose up in paradise before the dry lands [?], so too the river of God, which sprang up from the Father, is the Word;
and before us he shows myriads and countless rivers, and he enlightens the whole race of humankind.
Through the apostles, as by spiritual water, by their teaching, some in India are watered,
and some in Egypt, and others in the regions of Greece and Spain, and others elsewhere, and many gentiles.
This is what it says: "The course of the rivers gladdens the city of God; the Most High has sanctified his dwelling,"

which there he calls a city, and here he has given it the name holy dwelling of God the Most High; and he took up his dwelling among them and in their going, and "I will be their God, and they shall be my people."
God, the Almighty and Righteous, gladdened his church with the outflow of the rivers and made it a temple of God;
and he took up his dwelling in it and sanctified it, and watered it with spiritual teaching, and made it bear fruit through the practice of righteousness.
And God is in its midst at all times, for which reason the great king and prophet David has raised up a psalm, and sings and chants psalms and says:
"God is in their midst, and they shall not be moved." This is what God the Almighty said in the Gospel:
"Behold, I am with you at all times, even to the end of the world," and again:
"Wherever two or three gather for the sake of my name, I am there among them." "God will help it from morning to morning," he says, meaning very early and speedily.
And in various ways, beautifully, God brought his mercy and his help to them quickly, from morning to morning.
And the mercy of God came swiftly, first of all, and he says: "The nations trembled and kings were humbled; the Most High gave forth his voice, and the earth shook."
Of the coming of God's help he says: "The nations trembled and kings were humbled; the Most High gave forth his voice, and the earth shook."
The nations trembled and the wars of the enemies subsided, and to bring deliverance from bonds, "The Lord God of hosts is with us,
our upholder is the God of Jacob," for Jacob prophesied concerning the Church and said:
"A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his loins, until he comes who is the one awaited, and he is the hope of the nations."
Behold, after this they came, and his prophecies were fulfilled.
This is the one of whom David speaks at this time: "The Lord God of hosts is our upholder, and the God of Jacob."
The one of whom Jacob spoke at that time and prophesied, this is the God of Jacob.
Behold, the prophet David cries out and says: "Come and see the works of God, the wonders and signs he has done on the earth.
He has made war cease from end to end of the earth; he has broken bows, shattered weapons, and burned shields with fire.
Be still and understand that I am God; I am exalted among the nations and exalted on the earth."
He says this for every person to see, on account of which, very quickly and immediately, a change took place from evil to loftiness,
and from wrath to peace, and from ungodliness to righteousness, and from death to life, and from hell to the kingdom.
Because of all this, understand and see that I am God and the Creator of all created beings, and not of the Jews alone,
but also of all the nations, and the righteous one from end to end of the earth. And he is exalted and made manifest to all, and he has brought about deliverance.
Because of all this, the choir, the assembly of all the righteous and the believers and the apostles, has taken up a hymn together with David, crying out and saying:
"The Lord God of hosts is with us; our upholder is the God of Jacob."
Some people at that time said that this was about Gog and Magog, or about Ahaz, or else about Hezekiah and Sennacherib.
They spoke of this psalm in that way, but these men could not make war cease from end to end of the earth; rather, each one, according to his own power, took up only some part of it in likeness.
Or who made war cease and brought about peace, except the only-begotten Son of God alone, who made war pass away from end to end of the earth and made peace for the Church,
for just as the waves of the sea had their revels and upheavals at all its shores, with fierce winds, so the multitude of demons had engulfed all souls.
Truly the Lord has shattered the bows of evil godlessness; he has ground to powder, wiped out, and burned with fire all the shields and gates that were fighting against the Church.
These are the gates of hell, which cannot overcome the Church, for it is built upon the rock. Those who fell upon that stone
were broken to pieces, and on whomever it falls, it will crush him; for it shines with peace and piety, and they have taken hold of all the ends [of the earth].
This is the true interpretation of the word of the psalm.
Psalm 46. "For the end, for the sons of Korah." We have said many times what "the end" is, and we have shown what came about at the end of the times and was called the Church, for Paul says:
"In many parts and in many ways he spoke in former times through his prophets, but at the end of the times he spoke to us through his Son."
This is what it means when it says "for the end," for at the end of this world the Son came to his Church and established it.
As for the sons of Korah: they, and Asaph and Jeduthun, and others as well, were people with beautiful voices, choir leaders who sang praises,
who would raise their voices together with David, and by singing in concert with his voice would adorn it and would teach the choir,
for they were united in spirit by his grace, and they sang willingly, beautifully, and in harmony. This is what it means when it says "for the sons of Korah," and for Asaph and Jeduthun.
Now let us state the meaning and sense of the psalm, for this psalm was spoken concerning the deliverance of all the nations,
and how by victory all godlessness was swallowed up, and the only-begotten Son of God made great peace for his Church.
"Clap your hands, all you nations, and shout to God with a voice of joy, for the Lord is high and fearsome, and he is a great king over all the earth."
The prophetic word brings this forward and says that the company of the apostles and the assemblies of all the nations have been called to sing to God.
This is the gladness and joy of victory. It says: "Clap your hands, all you nations, and shout to God with a voice of joy."
The meaning of this psalm is in agreement with that one,
the one we discussed before this psalm, for there it mentioned tumult and trembling, and then it spoke of the victory and peace of the Church.
In the same way, this psalm saw the victory that was brought about by him, and it commands the whole company of the faithful, the assembly, to clap their hands,
to raise praise, to sing, and to say: "You, Lord, are high and fearsome, and the king is great over all the earth."
He has shown and made manifest to us, and "he has subjected peoples under us and nations under our feet, and he has chosen us as his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob, whom he loved."
Symmachus spoke with "the assembly" and says: "With the king is the beauty of Jacob, the beauty of his saints." Aquila speaks of it as the company of the apostles.
By saying this he shows that the righteous, the holy, and the faithful, arrayed for strengthening and for victory, sing with the clapping of hands.
This was seen at that time, which the prophet, seeing it with his eye, spoke of beforehand in words.
Now behold, it has been fulfilled, and the coming of the only-begotten Son of God has been accomplished, and that of his apostles, for bringing all the nations to faith.
And in only a little while the congregations and kings and nations submitted, and they taught them the psalm and song of the true God, to render song with glory, and the beauty of Jacob,
which he promised to the children of the righteous one, that the Gentiles would be blessed through them; this came about and was fulfilled through the only-begotten Son of God,
for at the time when he subjected himself for their sake, he brought the Gentiles and the godless to the hope of peace, to faith, and to the praise of God's glory.
And then it says: "God has gone up with blessing, and the Lord with the sound of the trumpet."
The one who says all this, who brings victory and peace to success, is the true only-begotten Son of God,
who became man and destroyed the nature of death and of the devil, and redeemed us and granted immortality to all people.
This is the true God, the only-begotten Son of God, who ascended to heaven in great victory and sent an angel to his holy apostles.
And he announced to them his coming once more in glory, and said to them: This Jesus, who ascended to heaven before you,
will likewise come once more in the glory of the Father, just as you saw him ascended to heaven.
As the Lord ascended to heaven, archangels and powers and principalities, dominions and authorities and myriads of myriads came out to meet him.
The ranks cried out, saying: "Lift up your gates, O rulers, on high, and let the eternal gates be lifted up, and the King of glory shall enter."
This they said in their various orders, beautifully and gloriously: "God has gone up with a shout, and the Lord with the sound of the trumpet." He went up on high with such singing.
After this came the union of the heavenly and the earthly; a multitude of angels came, saying together:
"Sing to our God, sing to our King, sing, for God is the great King over all the earth; sing to him with understanding.
God reigns over the Gentiles; God sits upon the thrones of his holiness."
Behold, with one voice those of heaven and those of earth offer spiritual praise to the almighty King,
for the true God gave glory to every person, and granted to those who believe in him to be sons of God, and glorified them, for all the Gentiles understood
that he is the true God, God and great King over all the earth, and that he sat down in glory at the right hand of the Father on high.
This is what it means when it says, "God sat upon the thrones of his holiness," for they were his, and it was not at that moment that he took possession of them.
Paul cries out in the same way, saying: "He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high." As for what it says, "Sing to him with wisdom":
it does not mean only with the breath of the voice and a shouting mouth, but with understanding and wisdom and inquiry and comprehension and thanksgiving for his lordship.
"The rulers gathered to the God of Abraham, for God's mighty ones of the earth were greatly exalted,"
for all the rulers of the Gentiles abandoned their ancestral gods and came to join the God of Abraham, and they became justified and children of Abraham.
Abraham became the father of many righteous people, for through his offspring the Gentile nations were blessed.
Those who knew the true God, their Creator, all came to the knowledge of God and glorified God.
Song was raised up from the earth, for by the power of God, with wisdom, they shattered the gates of hell and of death.
And he took away the tyranny of the devil and granted life and the kingdom to all, and he opened our mouth.
And all are to sing to God with a voice of joy. This is what it says: "Clap your hands, all you nations,
cry out to God with a voice of joy, for he is high and terrible, and a great king over all the earth."
Psalm 47, of blessing, of the sons of Korah. This psalm too, in the same manner as the previous one, recounts that God is great and mighty and victorious in battles:
"Great is the Lord, and greatly praised in the city of God and on his holy mountain." Indeed, we have said many times that the divine books have spoken of a city and a mountain.
It does not give this name to some single built structure, but applies it to the work of goodness and to the faith of holy people.
Now behold, it spoke at that time with glory of the Lord [?], and because from him and through him a city was built high and firm,
that is, the knowledge of God through faith, higher than all mountains, became a mountain, and all the righteous settled upon it as upon a city conspicuous and manifest.
The Lord explained this in the Gospel: "A city that is built on a mountain cannot be hidden."
"Firmly rooted, let all the earth rejoice," for by divine works it called "church" not only this built structure,
but it called firmly founded, and a spiritual rock, and a church, the teachers and the assembly of the righteous,
who were built upon the true divine faith in the only-begotten Son of God.
To this Paul testifies, saying: "You who are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, which is the foundation and the head of the corners,
our Lord Jesus Christ." And the Lord himself first blessed Peter and said to him:
"You are the rock, and on that rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not overcome it." This is what it calls firmly rooted,
that is, unshakable and invincible forever. "The mountains of Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great king."
High mountains surrounded Zion to be a shelter from the cold of the north,
that is, he guarded it from temptation, so that it may be unharmed by all godlessness from the face of the north.
The prophet speaks of evil being kindled upon the earth, and again he says: "They shall pursue you from the face of the north."
But the divine Zion Paul named spiritually a mountain, saying: "You have come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem."

He set strong mountains around it and drove away the north, and he guarded his city by the spiritual firmness of the apostles and of the saints and the righteous in unity with him, by the guarding from above of the bride, for it says thus:
"The camp of the angels of the Lord surrounds those who fear him and guards them." "God was made manifest in his holy temple at the time when he became a helper to them."
A single name is given to the catholic church throughout all sea and dry land,
for which reason we also say in our prayers, "for the holy and only catholic church from end to end of the earth," for it is fitting.
In many places and cities, in villages and country estates, the church is built, just as in one city many dwellings and houses are built,
and all of it is called one city. So likewise, if it is fitting, myriads upon myriads of countless and innumerable churches are built,
and they are called one word and one church, those who in truth and orthodoxy offer this temple to God.
Through all his mercies God made his help manifest to all; he bestowed it as a grace.
This is what it says: "God is made manifest in his holy temple at the time when he helps them."
Behold, concerning the wars and the rising up of kings against the prophets, behold, it says: "The kings of the earth gathered and came together.
They saw this and marveled." They sent men to war and saw the great victory, and they grew faint and were astounded, and they were afraid and were shaken.
"And trembling seized them; there was pain there, as of a woman giving birth.
With a fierce wind the ships of Tarshish were shattered." They saw the unshakable and firmly established foundation of the church.
They saw the prophets justified and fulfilled, and they were astonished with trembling and fear, as with the pain of a woman in childbirth,
or like a ship in the midst of the abyss of the waves. Thus those who had risen up against the churches to bring them down, having drawn near to death, spoke thus, crying out:
"As we have heard, so also have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God." That is, the word that we heard in our lawlessness,
now, behold, we have seen with our own eyes in the city of the Lord of the heavens and the city of our God, that is, the company of the holy believers of God.
"God has founded them forever." With the voice of the Lord himself it speaks of the building of the church upon this rock, and "the gates of hell shall not prevail against it."
He has taken up a psalm; the prophet sings with a great voice and says:
You who are redeemed by his redemption, sing psalms and tell it at all times, and say: "Receive your mercies in the midst of your people!"
And the word of the prophet was justified, was made complete and fulfilled, for thus our Savior says to his church:
"I am with you all days, even to the end of the world." "As is your name, O God, so also is your praise over all the earth."
Those who serve the false gods in vain, and whose idols, the things they made, were destroyed and blotted out and perished among them,
for they were false and empty: the song of the true God has filled all the ends of the earth.
"Your right hand is full of righteousness," O Lord; by the judgment of righteousness your right hand is mighty and has crushed your enemies.
"Let Mount Zion rejoice and let the daughters of Judah delight because of your judgments, O Lord." He calls the knowledge of God the height of Zion,
and he calls the daughter of Judah the churches of all the world, which came to faith by the hand of the apostles, who were of the race of the Jews, from whom they believed.
And all the Gentiles delight with joy, for the Lord of righteousness has been made manifest and has done away with perversity.
"Surround Zion and encompass it, and tell of its towers.
"Set your hearts on her strength and divide her towers!" Again he calls the goodness of piety Zion.
That is, he was strengthened by God's help, showed the earth the angelic way of life, and by his own effort set the tower of his justice around himself as a guard,
for the Holy Spirit graciously granted the redemption of the whole world and through his teaching established myriads of strong towers, for it says: "Select and divide her towers."
These are the leaders and teachers over the churches, and each one in his own time received this by lot and attained to it, and this not once or twice,
but God commanded many a generation of generations to serve as leaders and guardians:
"So that you may be able to tell it to another generation, for this is God, our God for ever and ever, and he will shepherd us for ever."
It is fitting, he says, for this to be told from generation to generation to the lawless and the unbelieving.
And just as we had that first tradition, so too generations relate the faith to generation, and the set-free [?].
In the preaching of every person [?], teach another generation also the knowledge that this is God, our God and Lord and good shepherd for ever and ever.
For it says, "Divide her towers," and through leaders and teachers it shows us that there is one chief shepherd,
who is the good shepherd and laid down his life for his sheep, and who shepherds not only by a single word,
by one only, the sheep [?], but protects all creatures, which were made to be of use for the sake of rational beings.
Psalm 48. For the end, of the sons of Korah. The company of all the apostles became mediator and evangelist to all the gentiles, and they have taken up singing of the faith of victory and teach it.
And in it they turned to the doing of goodness, despised all the glory of the world, counted it as vain, and despised folly, for that wisdom of theirs is folly and of very little worth.
And he says this beforehand, for the end, concerning the judgment and the recompense of each person according to his works, and he shows it to us.
Neither glory nor false gods can help a person in any way, but only deeds of purity and righteousness.
And for this reason its superscription says "for the end," that is, their recompense at the end according to their works. This is the sense and force of the psalm.
"Hear this, all nations, and heed me, all you who dwell in the world." Those who were no longer of Jewish kin: to them the prophet of God speaks.
Behold, he has raised the voice of proclamation and says: "Hear this,
all nations." I know that by grace and the Spirit the only-begotten Son of God gave us a mighty voice at that time, and through the apostles accomplished the redemption of all the ends of the earth,
for he speaks thus to the blessed company of the apostles: "Go and make disciples of all nations."
And not the Jews only, nor one people alone, but all the natures of men, "earth-born and sons of men together." Certain translators said
that the earth-born were Adam and Eve, for they were made from the earth, and that the sons of men were those who came from them.
But [?] their interpretation separates them from the truth, for he was preaching not about the dead, but about the living and those who walk upon the earth.
That is, these particular natures of men, who are alive at this time.
Let all your children after you hear this, each one for his own benefit, for himself:
"Be fruitful together, rich and poor," for the words of instruction teach us all and go before you.
"My mouth shall speak wisdom, and the meditations of my heart understanding.
I will incline my ear to a parable and will make known the parables of song" from the beginning, through your wisdom. All my speech is filled with the Holy Spirit.
Teach all people the hidden counsel and the commandments of the Lord our God; straighten the ears of all of you!
Hear with your hearing everything, just as my tongue has brought it forth in deed.
He makes this clear by saying: these words are not mine, but my tongue is held by the grace of God, like a pen.
And through him he counsels and speaks: he has been taken up, as one on behalf of another.
They put forward as evidence that our Lord spoke in parables to the crowd, but privately revealed everything to his disciples.
This psalm made such an opening statement: behold, it makes a beginning of its teaching: "Why should I not fear on the evil day?
The lawless deeds of my steps have surrounded me." The prophet has taken up what befalls our nature,
as, by questioning a sick person, he brings out from afar all his will and his recompense, and he speaks and relates: "Why should I not fear on the evil day?"
He calls the day of judgment upon sinners the evil day, for the apostle says:
"By your wickedness and by that unrepentant heart of yours you are storing up wrath for yourself.
The evil day is the revelation of God's righteous judgment," when "he will repay each person according to their deeds"; this is what he means when he says:
"Why should I not fear on the evil day?" For I look upon my lawlessness and the course of my deeds, and I shrink back from the judgment.
The prophet himself asks why he fears on the evil day.
And then he answers and says that it is because of the lawless deeds of his steps that he fears the judgment,
for "those who trust in their strength and boast in the abundance of their wealth"; behold, I am struck with dread and afraid because of the deeds of my steps,
but those who trust in their strength and their wealth have no strength at all, and they will carry away nothing on the day of judgment.
So they supposed and said, saying to themselves, that we will pay the price of wealth on the day of judgment for our evil.
Now, behold, he brings forward everything and shows us that there is no one who can redeem a person and renew him by works of righteousness, and he says:
"A brother cannot redeem, and a man cannot redeem, and he will not give God a ransom for himself, nor a payment as ransom for his own soul."
He instructs and teaches us that neither by kinship with those who are better,
nor as brothers of the good, nor can any people, through piety and righteousness, nor after the end, there on the day of judgment, can anyone at all be found who would be able to redeem.
For another prophet says that Noah and Job and Samuel cannot save their own sons and daughters.
And again, as for Noah and Daniel, it is well if they save their own souls.
All this was said because of those who live by doing evil and gather their wealth from their evil ways;
to these he shows by what work of goodness and righteousness they may redeem their soul.
"He shall labor forever and shall live completely, and he shall not see corruption, when the number of the wise see death,"
those who, moreover, endured sweat for the sake of piety and righteousness, for the sake of eternity.
They gladly accepted many afflictions, those who became firm in the hope of incorruptible life, and they have the fruit of their labors many times over, with great increase.
At a time of such sufferings and deaths, if, as he says, the righteous person is scarcely saved, where then will the ungodly and lawless person be found?
This is what he means when he says: "when the number of the wise see death."
That is, if affliction or death comes to the righteous, the ungodly will be found utterly destroyed.
This is what he means when he says: "Together the foolish and the wicked shall perish."
Symmachus translated it more clearly: "Together the speakers of vanity and the ignorant shall perish."
And he called speakers of vanity and foolish those who teach the evil wisdom of the world, by whose counsel they live their life wickedly.

This is what is meant by the saying that the wisdom of this world is madness with God, and "they shall leave their wealth to strangers, and their graves shall be their houses forever, their dwelling from generation to generation."
He speaks not only of the wise alone, but also of those who were stripped of their strength and power.
And at the end of their days, their dwellings and the houses they built remained deserted, like graves,
and strangers carried off their wealth; this is what he calls their dwelling from generation to generation.
After their death, they seized their fields and vineyards and gardens.
And they became an object of reproach, and people said this: This belonged to the family [?] of the one who unjustly seized from everyone.
Behold, he has taught us all: Do not exalt yourselves above your fellow passing mortal, but at all times accept closeness [?] according to nature.
"Man was in honor and did not understand; he imitated the senseless beasts and became like them."
This became the cause of his folly, for he did not want to understand and perceive his own honor and the dominion that God had graciously given him.
For this reason he became a beast and became a wild animal and took on a [?] life.
"This is the way of their life toward them," for he calls deeds a "way," and they were doing evil and folly and transgression of the commandments.
"After this they were pleased with their mouth," and after their end they received torment and wretchedness by their mouth,
those for whom the wealth of this world became no profit at all, and "like sheep they were given over to hell, and death shepherded them."
Symmachus translated this beautifully: "As sheep to slaughter, so they gave themselves over to hell of their own accord."
This is what he means: that of their own accord they prepared torments for their souls and passed from life to death.
"The upright ruled over them at dawn; their help wasted away in hell, and they fell from their glory," as has been said:
"The ungodly were diminished and fell when they saw the lawless man given into the hands of death and stripped of all his wealth."
The Lord explained all this to us by a parable in the Gospel, which he told about Lazarus and the rich man,
for they laid Lazarus in the bosom of Abraham, and he held lordship and reigned in the kingdom, while that commanding rich man was given over to bitter torment, to be burned.
From there he offered entreaty to Lazarus, and his entreaty was not made worthy of being heard.
So too, in the same way, the chant of the psalm has been raised after the end.
Then each one individually, after they have done this, offers entreaty to God, for to him alone belongs dominion, and after this he will no longer leave each one to his own will.
This is what he means by saying "only of God," for "he redeemed my soul from the hands of hell, when he receives me."
He speaks of the distress of the poor and of the hands of the powerful, he who at their end came to the poor as a helper, to console them and to give them relief:
"Do not be afraid when a man grows rich and the honor of his house is multiplied, for in his death he will not carry everything away with him, nor will the glory of his house go down with him."

But there is nothing more astonishing than how one who lives for five days, like a pampered child, begins to squander, and trusts in arrogance, and vaunts himself loftily in song, and schools himself in dissipation.
They call this one "of five days," for in keeping with this he adduces and says: "His soul will be blessed only in life."
As long as that rich man is still alive, some of the foolish call him blessed and long for what is his, but when he dies, they call him pitiable and give him the name of a poor man.
"He will give thanks to you when you do him good." Symmachus said this beautifully: "When a man's soul is rightly and truly good, he is praiseworthy;
those who are praiseworthy not only in their life but also at their end are the ones who use their wealth for the benefit of others."
But whoever takes his pleasure in this life alone, "he will enter the generation of his fathers, and he will not see light forever."
By "generation" he means a portion of earth: this will be his lot, eternal darkness will hold him back, and he will not see light.
Not only will he be kept back from this light, but he will not see light forever.
"Man was in honor and did not understand; he imitated the beasts and became like them."
This is the cause for those evildoers, who desired their own honor and rule more than the command of God.
They fell away from the honor and rule of God and became mortal and like the beasts, because they loved folly and despised wisdom.

Psalm 49, of Asaph. As the superscription has written, "A psalm of Asaph," it shows us this throughout the whole book of Psalms: that Asaph is the head of the choir of one group of those who sing praise.
But the heads of the choir of another canon are the sons of Korah, who with singing voice arrange the things spoken by their voice, and for this reason it says,
"A psalm of Asaph," because it was Asaph who would first take it up in voice and sing this psalm.
Then they would take up the voice and learn from him, and from him they would sing their hymn of praise with the choir of psalmists.
Now let us state the meaning of the psalm concerning the manifestation of our God and Lord Jesus Christ, and concerning the new covenant and law.
And again it teaches us that the worship and the sacrifices of the old law were subject to change, and nothing trustworthy to God or pleasing. "The God of gods,
the Lord, has spoken and called the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting." And since in the first psalm he calls every person to instruction,
in the same manner he called all from end to end of the earth, for it says, "from the rising of the sun to the setting."
This likewise is a sign: "God of gods." He calls God mighty and great and true; rightly he calls him God and leader of teachers and rulers.
In another place too it says: "God stood in the assembly of the gods."
Moses explained this to us: "You shall not despise your God, and you shall not revile the ruler of your people."
For he called them gods whom he appointed in his own likeness as rulers and leaders.
"Out of Zion is the beauty, the salvation of his comeliness." By this he means God, who was manifested at this time.
He is the one who from Zion showed us his beauty and comeliness, and at this time, the greater salvation and the comeliness of his wonder, he was manifested and accepted the sufferings of his flesh.
And indeed another, Solomon, says: "He is beautiful to behold, more than the sons of men," and "Our God shall come openly, and our God shall not keep silent."
Do not suppose that he will keep silent as at the first coming, for the first time, through our nature, he was hidden and silent in his own glory and in the great beauty of his divinity,
for truly in his love for humankind he graciously granted to all redemption and the forgiveness of sins.
But at the second coming he manifested his judgment and kingship, and he will no longer be long-suffering; swiftly he will summon all, to judge each person according to his own deeds.
This is what it says: "Our God shall not keep silent; fire shall blaze up before him, and around him great gusts of wind."
This same thing blessed Daniel saw: a river of fire, he says, flowing before him, and his throne like a flame of fire, and the wheels of his chariot like flashes of fiery lightning.
"He shall summon the heaven above, and the earth, to judge his people."
And the lawgiver, blessed Moses, did likewise, and gathered the Jews to him, and called heaven as witness:
"Give heed, O heaven, and I will speak, and let the earth hear the words of my mouth." In the same way Isaiah too said at the beginning of his prophecy:
"Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken."
This is not as if to rational beings or to living creatures, but in order to strike with dread and to rebuke, for the sake of human beings, the senseless mountains [?].
They took upon themselves with honor the bearing of God's command; how much more should the peoples who have ears fulfill the commands of God.
In the same way blessed Abraham set apart seven ewe lambs and dug a well as a testimony. In the same way Jacob and Laban called upon the hills as witness.
"To gather to him his saints and those who offer the sacrifice of the covenant upon the altar. The heavens declared his righteousness, for God is judge."
As we said earlier, he shows us the terror of that judgment, and also that the fulfillment of the law and the offerings were of no need to God, as he says.
He calls holy Moses and Aaron and Eleazar and Phinehas, who after them served as priests in holiness,
and he commands that they be gathered: "Let these look to me" by means of the law; and then afterward he brings the fulfillment of the new covenant.
The heavens declared that God is judge in justice. He gave the name "heaven" to the heavenly powers.
"Hear, my people, and I will speak to you." And he shows us which people: "And, Israel, I will testify to you."
And God shows us his own domain: "I am your God," who formerly brought you out of Egypt,
who granted you passage on dry land through the midst of the sea and your nurture in the wilderness, who gave the law of the old covenant.
Do not count me as another! Now at this time I am the one I was at that time.
"It is not for your sacrifices that I rebuke you, for your calves are always before me."
He says: "It is not your offerings that I seek; I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flock.
Mine is every beast of the forest, the wild animals of the mountains and all the cattle. I know the birds of the sky, and the beauty of the fields is with me."
He says: I am the creator and lord of all things, both of the living creatures of the dry land and of all the birds.
Do not reckon or suppose that I fulfill any wish of mine through an offering of gold. I am the one who graciously gave you that and everything else.

It was I who made the beauty of fruit-bearing trees spring up from the earth; and since the creatures of the dry land supply offerings and calves, goats and sheep, and the birds supply dove and turtledove,
and those that bear sweet fruit supply wine and oil, and the fragrant plants supply incense, for all this reason I will silence all your offerings and sacrifices.
"If I should be hungry, I would not tell you." He says: Even if it were needful to me, I would have no longing for anything of yours, for all creatures are mine.
Now God speaks of the absence of any deficiency in his nature: "I do not eat, he says, the flesh of your calves, nor do I drink the blood of your goats."
From the childishness and youth of your law I now move you to perfection; I lay down the law of the new covenant, which it is fitting to offer to me.
"Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, pay your vow to the Most High, and call on me in the day of your affliction; I will deliver you, and you will glorify me."
The Holy Trinity was revealed here. For he did not say one God,
nor one sacrifice of praise, but he showed us the distinctness of each one individually, and God on high and the benefactor, and the sacrifice that fulfills the new law.
And for the sacrifice of praise is the prayer and blessing of the righteous, and for in the twentieth
psalm he says earlier: "I will fulfill my vow before all who fear him," for he said above:
"It is not for your sacrifices that I judge you." I will show you, he says, for what I reprove you.
"But to the sinner God said: 'Now how do you speak of my righteous decrees, and take up my covenant in your mouth,
for behold, you have hated instruction, and have put away from you and scattered all the words of my mouth.'"
For those who were among the teachers and leaders, who were somewhat learned, and the priests,
themselves doers of worse things, walked in filth and taught others the divine scriptures, while they themselves were transgressors of the commandments.
To such teachers he speaks thus: How have you shown yourself a man of knowledge, and how do you recount and teach the divine scriptures, to their abasement?
Those scriptures that can be of profit to me, you did not believe, and you make the divine scriptures an object of reproach; you teach others, and you yourself by your deeds trample them underfoot.
Now let me count up your transgressions as well: "If you saw a thief, you ran along with him, and you placed your portion with harlots;
your mouth multiplied evil and your tongue contrived deceit; you sat and spoke evil against your brother, and you laid a stumbling block for your mother's son."
[?] Very harsh are your rash deeds, likened to you, according to the word of the apostle:
"You who say not to steal, you steal; you who say not to fornicate, you fornicate."
He recounts all the other lawlessness: "You who teach others do not teach yourself," and "for you have transgressed and you dishonor the law of God."
Now he says: "By his own long-suffering I measure out countless long-suffering; on account of the heart [?] I am long-suffering beyond measure even toward doing evil."
"All this you did, and I kept silent toward you. You suppose indeed in your lawless heart that I am just like you."
I have seen all your rash deeds, and I was long-suffering toward you, in case perhaps you might come to uprightness and repentance.
And my long-suffering I made [?] the occasion of your evil, and you did not reckon it a grace, nor did you repent.
"Now I will reprove you and set all this before you," since you did not understand, he says, the sweetness of my long-suffering.
He joined this saying to the saying of the apostles, that "the kindness of your God leads you to repentance."
But by that hardness of yours and your unrepentant heart you store up wrath for yourself for that day
when the just judgment of God will be revealed, who repays each person according to their deeds.
In this way he threatens, and again in his love for humankind he shows us, and as if with threats, he summons them with a calling in order to instruct them.
"Understand this, all you who have forgotten God, lest he somehow snatch you away and there be no one to deliver you."
He says: Let each one of you strive for this on behalf of your soul, while you have not yet been snatched away by death, for death snatches away every person,
like a lion, and no one is able to be rescued from its hands. Now, after this, he makes the beginning of the new law of this psalm,
which he shows us in an ornate and beautiful manner: "The sacrifice of praise will glorify me. And there is the way where I will show them my salvation."
Symmachus said this beautifully: "By the help of praise he was glorified. To those who walk in integrity he showed the salvation of God."
He speaks not only of one thing, the praise of God and the offering of the sacrifice of praise, but also of the accomplishment of goodness.
Again, let a person accomplish integrity by action conformed to his own life, and in this way it is possible to attain the salvation of God; by faith and deed all righteousness is accomplished,
by which all this was filled and fulfilled through the new law, which the only-begotten Son of God graciously granted to all.
Psalm 50. For the end, a psalm of David, when Nathan came to him,
when David had gone in to Bathsheba. The superscription of the psalm shows us this beautifully and wisely, and the word of the psalm also bears witness to it,
but it must be recognized that it approaches prophecy and begins to speak, for the superscription calls it a psalm "for the end."
This shows us the order of the end, of the new law, and teaches its service.
First the psalm speaks of repentance, so that he might blot out our sins, and at the same time it also reached prophecy, for it says this:
"Do not take your Holy Spirit from me." He prepared and arranged his own medicine of repentance and taught many others,
and he became a guide, so that those who sin may learn from the words of the psalm and find blotting out for themselves:
"Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy, and by your many compassions blot out my lawlessness."
Now he speaks of his own desires and speaks in figures of the Babylonian captivity, and on behalf of that people he confesses his own sins, and them, himself, together with
himself [?], and likewise, for those very great sins and harms and severe wounds, he applies that great medicine upon the wound.
And through excessive desire they had fallen away from God's love for humankind.
And it must be said that the sins were harsh, but they could not overcome your love for humankind.
Therefore he says: "Wash me further from my lawlessness and cleanse me from my sins."
I know that by the hand of the prophet you rebuked me and granted the remission of my sins. I know that you cut out and cauterized.
Now, by your great mercy, lay your compassion upon that wound, and remove the stench that comes from the [?] of sins, and cleanse it from me, and heal me, wound and all, by your love for humankind,
"For I know my lawlessness, and my sin is ever before me."
I know, Lord, that if it be fitting, by your many mercies you will blot out my sins.
But I remember them at all times, and I see them as though they were written out before me.
By night they secretly come upon me in visions, and by day they torment me with thoughts. The great king David had learned to do this from the divine books, for Isaiah says thus:
"You will not be justified from the first of your iniquities." In agreement with this, in the thirty-first
psalm blessed David says: "I said, I will tell my iniquity to the Lord;
you forgave me all my impieties," and "Against you alone have I sinned, Lord, and done evil before you."
If it is fitting to say so, my sins concerning Uriah and Bathsheba are grievous.
And for all that [?] of his and for the sin that I committed against you, and I transgressed and did it before you, who were their creator.
This is what he means when he says: "Against you I have sinned, Lord, and done evil before you, so that I may be justified by your word and you may prevail in your judgment."
By my own doing harm came upon me, and you rightly found me deserving of judgment. That is, because Nathan reproved him.
You revealed my hidden deeds and granted me your love for mankind. Thus you are just in all things.
With every person you show your mercy: you reprove, you instruct, and you receive them in your love for mankind.
"Behold, in iniquity she conceived, and in sin my mother bore me."
Likewise the opening word [?]: before a person comes into being and even before birth, he says, they began to sin, to commit iniquity and to be cursed,
for after the transgression of the commandment God punished man and drove him out of paradise, and he became mortal and close to the curse.
And then it says further: "Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain."
And he says that sin entered the world before birth, and through sin they became offspring of the curse.
And blessed Paul says this: "Through a man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus every person entered into death, because all have sinned."
And for this reason God said: "Every mind of man is inclined to hold fast to evil from his youth and all the days of his life."
Beware of those heretics who say that the nature of sin is abiding, for did not human nature sin first?
Because it was created free, it committed sin willingly, and for this reason it was punished.
So sin does not exist by nature; rather, human nature is able to do whatever it wishes.
God made it immortal and good and free, and of its own will it committed sin, and for sin it received death as punishment. And this is what he means when he says:
"Behold, in lawlessness she conceived, and in sin my mother bore me."
For they became corruptible and only then bore offspring, likewise corruptible and close to sorrow and pains. Man fought against this in thought
at all times, against iniquity and against sin, and through great struggle the saints found victory, and in return for victory they won the crown of glory.
"You, Lord, have loved truth," and, he says, you are a just and true judge: to some you give punishment as torment, and to others a crown of glory,
for you truly repay each person according to their deeds, and you look upon the weak mind, and to those who repent you graciously grant forgiveness.
"The unseen and hidden things of your wisdom you have revealed to me."
He says: I, who have received so much grace from you: not only did you give me kingship, but you also bestowed on me the grace of prophecy.
And the things that were hidden from others you showed to me openly, the things that were to come about in future and later times.
And to others I proclaimed the incarnation of your only-begotten Son, and that he redeemed us from the passions, and the resurrection from the dead,
and to all the world great grace, and birth from above from the baptismal font by the hand of the Holy Spirit,
and the forgiveness of all sins. And all those to whom this was granted became children of God.
All this I learned from your Holy Spirit, for which reason I entreat you and offer up sighing, for I have sinned, and afterward may I find grace with your beneficence.
But according to your great mercy, by your immeasurable love for humankind, send upon me the grace of your Holy Spirit, as it was at first,
for which reason I cry out and call and say: "Sprinkle me with your sprinkler, wash me, cleanse me, and I shall be made whiter than snow."
He says this prophetically before the Gospel, and by the grace of baptism he grants such washing and cleansing to all through the baptismal font.
For this reason he says this by the hand of the prophet Isaiah: "Wash yourselves, cleanse yourselves."
And after this he says: "And if your sins are like purple, wickedly, the color of [?],
I will make them white as snow, and if they are as if dyed with scarlet, I will make them white as wool."
This is because, according to the Law, those sins that were very great were not answerable to [?] the hope of the sprinkling of blood with hyssop, but to the penalty of death.
For this reason the prophet entreats: Do not judge me according to the Law, he says, and do not put me to death as of old,
but by the grace of the new Law sprinkle me, and cleanse me with the blood of your only-begotten Son and with the life-giving Spirit,
and let it not be the punishment of the written Law, death, but "Make me hear song and joy, and my humbled bones shall rejoice."
He says this: "Give me joy to hear with my ears, and if you grant me fulfillment, holiness and righteousness,
let all my flesh rejoice; let them together take up strength and be filled with the spirit of your grace.
And I will raise a divine song with my mouth, and I took up the lyre to sing, and I said: "Who shall tell of the mighty acts of the Lord and make all his praises heard?"
"Turn your face away from my sins and blot out all my iniquities."
But look upon my solitude, he says, and remove from me that doubt of sin, and put all my sins far from your face, he says.
"Create a pure heart in me, O God, and renew an upright spirit in my body," for this reason: show me your love for humankind and grant the forgiveness of my sins.
But establish in me a pure heart, for I have received it, and further keep me from evil thoughts.
He said this by the hand of Ezekiel, when Ezekiel was with those captives of Babylon: "I will give them a new heart and a new spirit."
He does not speak of the spirit in every case as of the Holy Spirit, but of this spirit of speech of ours, which is the directing [?] of fornication [?].
Is this what he means when he says: teach and become guides, with your heart and with the spirit of speech, as rightly directed guides and as those who bring forth fruit?
Thus at this time, here, blessed David says: My heart is afflicted and corrupted, but "create in me a pure heart" of speech,
so that I may speak and do the thoughts of your truth; "Do not cast me away from your presence, O Lord, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me."
By this he made clear that everything that was done, all of it, was by the holy grace of the Spirit.
It is not that God could not have removed it from him, but he entreats and asks in this way as though it were his own.
And he entreats him not to remove it from him, so that the order of prophecy may be made manifest, the keeping of which he learned by the practice of righteousness and by walking in the way of peace.
"Give me the joy of your salvation and establish me with your governing spirit." I beseech you, he says, deliver me from the slavery of sin
and make me free, and with the spirit of governance, that is, call me to the royal mystery, and may I be freed from those to whose slavery I was joined, and from that evil one.
My intention is that by the spirit of speech I may be unashamed, and that by its authority I may speak candidly: may my walking be with understanding.
"I will teach the lawless your ways, and the ungodly will turn to you."
I became, he says, a guide and teacher of those who have sinned, he says, and who wish to turn back and repent.
I became their preacher, that I might tell them of mercy and great love for humankind, and I turned many ungodly to you.
And he will see the blotting out of my many sins, and will flee with sighing and repentance to the gates of your mercy.
"Deliver me from blood, O God, God of my salvation," he says. He repeatedly recalls the murder of Uriah; at first he only mentioned it and said:
"I know my lawlessness, and my sin is before me always, at all times." Let us come now to what follows.
And let us approach what has been appointed. He says: "My tongue will sing of your righteousness." Symmachus translated this as follows:
"Let my tongue meditate on your mercies; may I never keep silent, he says, about this great benefaction of yours done to me by you, but with blessing may I praise your great graces."
"Lord, if you open my lips, my mouth will declare your praise," because sin has stopped my mouth, he says, and has bound my tongue to my palate,
he says. But the prophet entreats; he asks for his former boldness, so that he may move his tongue to sing to God.
"If you had wished a sacrifice to be offered to you, you did not want a burnt offering."
The psalm that came before this one was joined to this psalm, for there it says:
"I will not accept young bulls from your house, nor goats from your flock"; and blessed David had heard this from God, and rightly said here:
"If you had desired a sacrifice to be offered to you — burnt offerings did not please you." You said that you will not accept dumb beasts and cattle as sacrifice and burnt offering from me.
By the hand of the priests he says: "But the sacrifice to God is a humble spirit. And a humble and holy heart and spirit the Lord will not despise."
He says: a priestly and great offering and a faithful sacrifice is if someone brings and offers it before me with the humility of his heart and with the pure intention of all his thoughts,
and himself bears a likeness to it in all humility, just as the blessed three youths in the furnace spoke, saying:
"With a humbled head and a spirit of poverty may we be offered, as burnt offerings and sacrifices of bullocks and as myriads of fitting lambs."
So let this our sacrifice be offered before you today. For the text of this psalm is like that prayer and supplication of those who were captives in Babylon;
in like manner he speaks and recounts, for like the blessed three youths, they in this same way offered themselves and their prayers to God as sacrifice and burnt offering.
And they needed no other bullock or goat, but with humility and their poverty, of their own will, they offered themselves with joy as a sacrifice to God.
"Do good, O Lord, in your will to Zion, and let the walls of Jerusalem be built!
Then you will be pleased with the sacrifice of righteousness, offering and burnt offering; then bullocks will be offered upon your altar."
Here, after this, he mentioned the Babylonian captivity, because he longed for liberation from slavery.

And he entreats God for going to Jerusalem and for seeing the temple with joy, and for serving the Law with burnt offerings and bullocks, and for the great boast of the priests, the praise of righteousness, to sing and to say:
"If you open my lips, then my mouth will declare your praise," for David himself said in another place:
"How shall I praise you with the praise of the Lord in a foreign land?" For this reason there is also another sense of the prophecy.
At that time the sacrifice of righteousness will please him: they will not offer cattle as an offering to him, but rational and living beings will be offered in righteousness upon the altar of God.
Of this the blessed Paul says: "I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, take care to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, pleasing to God, this your rational service."
The divine David knew, for the unrevealed and hidden things of the wisdom of God had been revealed to him,
and he knew how by the Law grace is fulfilled for the remission of all sins, and immortality and life.
We find that rational and speaking beings are offered upon the altar of God, joined together with the blotting out of sins.
All this he said prophetically, and it was fulfilled.
Psalm 67, for the end, of David, spoken by Saint Epiphanius of Cyprus. The blessed David had seen the evil deeds of men and the tyrannical rule of the devil, and through the all-holy Spirit he hoped
for the manifestation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and for the benefits and gains that were to come to the world through him, and for how human nature was delivered from death and rescued from tyranny.
and let them glorify the God of all. Taken together, he speaks of the new covenant and of the great wonders that have been graciously given to this world.
For all of this he has raised up a song, and he sings psalms and teaches us with this psalm:
"Let God arise and let all his enemies be scattered, and let those who hate him flee from before his face." And bring it to fulfillment, you
who are Lord of all, by graciously granting your salvation to each and every person.
For this reason he says that all the enemies, as soon as they see this, will turn to flight.
Here he speaks of rising up as opposed to the long-suffering of God, since vengeance was to take place and righteous judgment was to come. Now he entreats him to arise, that is to say:
Be long-suffering no longer toward the evil tyrant and the enemy of our life, but bring his rule to an end, put death to death, and crown life.
"As smoke vanishes, so let them vanish, and as wax melts before the fire, so let sinners perish from before the face of God."
Just as smoke cannot withstand the wind, nor wax the fire,
so likewise neither the tyranny of the devil nor his power can withstand the manifestation of the Word of God,
but at his manifestation alone they turn to flight, and those who do not believe in God are made ready by just judgment for torment, and the righteous rejoice.
All this came about for the company of the righteous: filled with joy, they have raised up a song and they bless God:
"Let the righteous rejoice and be glad before him; let them exult with joy." He has shown us all this,
that this is not a victory by human action, but this glory is from God, for by our understanding [?] he has graciously granted redemption to the whole world.
And all who are worthy of him are glad and truly bless God. For this reason he likewise takes up and says:
"Bless God and sing to his name; and make a way for him who sits upon the west, and Lord is his name, and let them rejoice before him."
Here by prophecy he shows us the company of the apostles, who were sent out into all the world and made all people ready to praise the great King.
And the Lord himself shows us openly and says:
"Go and make disciples of all the nations, and baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit."

And by that teaching of baptism and of birth from above, a right and straight way came into being, and all his believers came to dwell in a house and temple of the Holy Spirit, and the Lord of all is with them as their fellow traveler.
For this reason the prophet says in a vision: "Make a way for him who sits upon the west; Lord is his name."
He speaks of the west for this reason: because people by their own doing removed themselves from the true light and sat in darkness and the shadows of death.
But now, behold, the sun of righteousness has appeared and has done away with the darkness of gloom, and in its place he has prepared his temple and dwelling, this
is human nature; those who sat in the darkness of the west, having risen up, saw a great light and recognized the Savior, their Lord.
"Be shaken with dread before his face, he who is the father of orphans and the judge of widows."
This is that by which all the services of the demons trembled and were thrown into confusion.
And this we have learned from the holy Gospel, for the demons cried out with shouts and said: "What is there between us and you, Jesus, Son of God?
You have come before the time to torment us." This is what it means when it says, "Tremble before his face."
He became a father of orphans and set free the captives and the afflicted from the tyranny of the devil: "God in his holy place."
For it said, "Let God arise," and again: "Make way for him who sits toward the west."
Baruch says: "God, in his holy place," so that no one should suppose that the nature of the Godhead admits of changing from place to place;
but this whole saying clearly shows us his appearing as one who labors and contends,
for the Word was with the Father and lived openly among human beings in his own flesh, and was not separated from the Father.
"God settles those of one manner in a house, and leads out the bound by his strength, and likewise those who embittered him, who had fallen asleep in the tombs."
By "of one manner" he means one faith, those who live in goodness and good order, and not those of whom some held things one way and some another.
Rather, those of one manner should walk in one truth and follow the knowledge of the Lord. Such people shall dwell in the house of God.
And he set free the bound, those who were bound by sin, and once freed from their bonds they performed very great deeds of courage.
Such was Matthew the tax collector, such was James son of Alphaeus, such was Zacchaeus the righteous, and they gained a good name, they who had been bound to the devil.
He showed great power, and he is not speaking of one bond only.
Rather, those who were still lying buried in godlessness and lawlessness, as if in a tomb, such people he set free and liberated.
"O God, when you went out before your people and when you passed through into the wilderness, the earth shook, for the heavens dripped."
Symmachus put this more beautifully: "O God, when you went out before your people and when you dwelt in the wilderness, the earth shook, and by your severity at that time the heavens dripped."
What is this that it says, "at your manifestation"? At your dwelling in the wilderness, an uninhabited [?] light that no one has ever seen.
All this came to pass at the time of the crucifixion. Then the earth shook and the rocks were split.
And after the ascension the heavens poured down the grace of the Holy Spirit like a heavy rain, the dew of blessing.
And he granted the apostles the knowledge of tongues, by which they converted and saved all the ends of the earth and taught the Jews well.
And it says: "from the face of the God of Sinai, before the face of the God of Israel," for the one who was at Sinai is the very one it calls the God of the fathers in those first times;

behold, today he has made manifest his love for humankind, and suffered in our nature, and accomplished redemption, and by change and shaking he rebuked the Jews and bestowed the grace of the Holy Spirit on all the world.
"A voluntary rain, O God, you prepared for your inheritance"; for what it says there, "the heavens dripped," also showed the dew of blessing of the new covenant by your inheritance.
These are his believers. "And though it grew weak, you strengthened it," for they grew weak, fell sick, and rose up.
And trials and battles came upon the saints. Likewise the Lord says to Paul: "My grace is great for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness,"
Although trials and afflictions come upon the saints from time to time, in a little while he strengthens them and gives them courage and grants them victory.
And through them he filled all his inheritance with the grace of his teaching, for in another place David prophesies and says:
"Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and all the ends of the earth for you to possess." "Your wild beasts also dwell in it."
Here he called the apostles God's wild beasts, each of whom was turned into a wild creature, and through them people were brought to the knowledge of God.
So Paul was wild in the manner of a beast; he brought him by seizing him, as one seizes a wolf, and made him ready as a chosen vessel, for he says thus:
"He is a chosen vessel for me, so that he may hold my name high before all the nations and kings and all the sons of Israel."
And again the prophet Habakkuk speaks of the apostles as steeds and horses: "Your steeds shall go upon the sea, stirring up the many waters of the deeps,"

for the swords went out over all the earth, and they were steeds of the Holy Spirit, and they charged against those many gods and destroyed the terrified idols, and they established the church in all the ends of the earth.
"In your sweetness, O God, you made ready for the poor one!" Human nature was weak and poor and sick.
You saved it by your sweetness and prepared for it every rest and glory.
"The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the good news with great power." Above he named the apostles beasts, but here he called them proclaimers of the good news,
for some were hunters and some tax collectors and some tent-makers, and they became teachers over philosophers and sages and orators and over all who were learned in wisdom.
Now show me where such power in them came from. He says that the Lord gave them power. Those who proclaim the good news with great power.
"The King of the powers of your beloved, the beauty of your house and the dividing of the spoil."
He says King of powers, for our Lord Jesus Christ is King, and the apostles are his powers and his beloved, for so our Lord called them in the Gospel:
"You are my beloved ones; from now on you shall no longer be called servants, but friends."
Likewise Paul says: "Who will separate us from that love of God: persecution or distress [?]?"
That is to say, however many trials come upon us, the devil is unable to snatch us away,
nor to separate us from the love of Christ. Rather, being strengthened, we have overcome the devil and cast down his fierce ones.
For he says thus: "If God is on our side, who is there to speak evil against us?"

"The beauty of your house, the dividing of the spoil." By the grace of the Holy Spirit he established the assembly of believers well and enlightened it, and abundantly granted the dividing of the spoil,
for this is the division of the apostles: some to Rome, some to the Ionians, and some to Egypt,
and they took spoil with great force and struggle, and they snatched people away from the error of idolatry and brought them to the knowledge of God, and they guided us well, and may he teach us [?].
"If you sleep among the lots: the wings of a dove covered with silver, and the middle of her back with the color of gold."
By the wings of the dove he means the Gospel and the grace of the Holy Spirit, which came down in the likeness of a dove upon the waves of the Jordan.
The wings are covered with silver on account of the time of the proclamation to all of God the Savior; for he says: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him."
And again he says the same in another psalm: "The words of the Lord are pure words, like silver refined and tested in the earth."
These are the wings, the wings of the dove covered with silver, and the middle of her back with the color of gold.
He has indicated to us the invisible and hidden, all-knowing nature of the Godhead, for the Lord says in the holy Gospel:
"My words are also from me [?]," for by the sinless and holy and unswearing [?] hands of the labor of his own flesh he enlightened
the words of their minds, and made them shining, silver-colored, and easy for all to hear, through the practice of good teaching.
And they feed milk to the imperfect and the ignorant by the hand of the holy apostles, but to the perfect, and to those who were able to reach the depth, he gave solid food.
This is the middle of the back with the color of gold. Blended on high, it reveals that divine lowliness of which Paul says: "We speak wisdom among the perfect."
"If you sleep among the lots" of the all-immaculate one, the grace of the Holy Spirit does not approach in vain, but those who at all times are with him [?].
And he called them always at rest, "If you sleep," for the graces of the Holy Spirit are unmoved and unshaken among the lots.
By "lot" he means his own Old and New Testament. If you have heard, God has graciously given us both Testaments, and through them the great light of knowledge.
"When the one who is in heaven appointed kings over it, they were made white as snow on Selmon."
Here he gave his apostles the name of kings, for in the forty-fourth psalm he calls them rulers: "And he appointed them rulers over all the earth."
He prophesies, before the coming of the Holy Spirit, which took place at the feast of Pentecost, which is Martvilia [?],
how it was upon that assembly of the holy apostles, and how grace rested upon each of them and planted knowledge among them.
At that time he gave them the division of all the ends of the earth, and kingship.

To some the eastern part, and to some the western part, and to others many other places he commanded them to sanctify and to cleanse; and they carried out the washing of their [?] and made them white as snow.

Beforehand he prophesied about the place as Selmon, and by Selmon he indicates to us the city of Jerusalem and makes it clear that there the company of the holy apostles received the power of the Holy Spirit.
"Mountain of God, rich mountain, curdled mountain"; just as he sometimes calls the apostles a chariot, and sometimes evangelists and rulers and kings,
so also here he gave the apostles the name of mountain, by this saying in the Gospel: "A city that is built on a mountain cannot be hidden."
And again Isaiah cries out and says: "On that last day the mountain of the Lord will be revealed as a rich and curdled mountain."
He gives order to all the faithful and to those who have settled in the teaching of the apostles.

This is the one around which the angels are stationed and drawn up for the church; joined with one another they keep guard, and with them they have the spiritual food of holy grace, through the richness of God.
"What do you suppose, you proud mountains?" But Aquila said this:
Why have you, you turbulent mountains, set yourselves against the mountain "on which it pleased God to dwell," along with those Jews?
Through the prophets he sent his words, also to the heretics and the lawless who had gone astray, that his own house, that very house, [?] as his temple and church.
But here he says this about it: that "the Lord too will dwell in it completely and until the end of time."
He does not say this in the way that he once called the temple of the Jews a temple, and from then on no longer named it his own.
Do not suppose this about the church; rather, in this one he has dwelt completely and until the end of time.
"The chariots of God are ten-thousandfold, and thousands lead them forward." He is not speaking of that Jewish holiness, which they supposed to be God's resting place,

but of myriads upon myriads and many thousands, the assemblies: God established the church as a resting place, to take up his dwelling by his Holy Spirit, and he promised to give it a crown of glory and an unfading kingdom.
"The Lord is among them in holy Sinai." This is the one who at that time appeared to your fathers at Sinai.
This is the very same one who sends the chariots at this time in his church;
and it is not that that one was someone else and this one another; he is the same, the Lord himself, who leads all in fullness.
