In every way the prophet shows us this: that he came down, broke the tyranny of wars, set free those who had formerly been taken captive, and granted them freedom.
"He ascended on high and led captivity captive": he shows us the ascent, for he came down, and Paul the apostle is witness to it.
What then is that ascent, if not that he descended to the lower parts of the earth?
He who came down is the same who ascended above the highest places; he led captivity captive and took captives;
those who were captives of the devil he seized for life, and, delivering them from the tyranny and slavery of the devil, he granted them freedom and the blotting out of sins.
"He took captives and divided them as gifts to the sons of men."
They took up the spoil, people found faith, and they were made rich, sons of God, and the kingdom of good things was granted to them, "so that it might be a dwelling place even for the unbelieving."
He did not look, it says, on that former pagan, devilish lawlessness in which they had been; rather, they found faith, and he says:
"Today, if they hear my voice, every good thing will be granted them." "The Lord God is blessed; blessed is God day by day."
Baruch prophesies and sings, announces the glory of God to all, and says:
The praise of God is fitting at all times, for he has granted us such love for humankind.
"May the God of our salvation make our way prosper," he who has saved all of us and directed our paths in righteousness.
It says: "Our God is a God who saves," for he himself is the source of good things.
He it is who gave us life to drink. "From the Lord are the ways out of death."
For he opened for me the gate of hell that had been shut against us, and he shattered its bronze doors and iron bolts.
And the Lord himself brought about deliverance from death, and he delivered me from the darkness of the pit and led me to life.
"God will shatter the heads of his enemies, hair and skin together, those who walk in their lawlessness."
He tells us: he opened the gates of hell and "made a way out of death, and he broke open and shattered the crowns of the heads of his enemies."
And he left nothing among them, not even so much as a single hair, without exact scrutiny, but carried the investigation down to its very foundation.
This is the "hair with the skin," and he did not let it go until, by the judgment of his justice, he had repaid everything in full measure. What is this that he is saying?
For he left not even a small fault without exact scrutiny, since he saw that the audacity of the devil was guilty in every respect,
that audacity which dared to send [death] upon the Lord's flesh, the holy, spotless and blameless flesh, which he had from our nature.
The Lord of all, like all others, entered into a contest with death.
The Savior says this in the Gospel: "The ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me."
But although he found nothing to match his audacity, the devil nevertheless sent [death] upon the Lord's flesh and gave it over to death.

This is what it means when it says: "He shattered the heads and the hair with the skin," for in the matter in which he had been audacious, he repaid everything with minute scrutiny and punished the devil and death,
which is his dominion, and the lover of humankind in his mercy undid and shattered the gates of hell.
He led out the human mind and rescued it from death, and graciously granted it the gift of freedom and salvation.
The Lord said: "I will turn them back from the depths and abysses, and from the unyielding bolts and from the gates of destruction I will bring them out."
That is: he delivered our ruined nature from sin and lawlessness and from the midst of death,
granted us life, brought us out, and seated us at the right hand of God, "that your feet may be dipped in blood, and the tongues of your dogs in the blood of your enemies."
He has taken up a figure and shows us by what battle the tyrant was defeated. And his dominion, that is, death, was brought to nothing,
and he assigns certain of the Gentiles the name of dogs, for he gave them death to trample underfoot and gave them the head of the dragon as food.
Isaiah explains this same thing to us and says: "I filled a single winepress and trod it with my strength, and I crushed it in my wrath, and [?] spattered my garment."
He says something further after this: "Your goings have appeared, O God, the goings of our God and holy King,"
He gives the name "goings of God" to the ministry of the holy King, for he sprang from the summits of a holy and royal lineage.
"The rulers hastened to the offering of song among the virgins who give praise."
Here, after this, he has raised the song of praise of the New Covenant and concerning the order of the Church;
he sings psalms, and they taught all people to give glory with joy. And he calls the apostles "princes," for they became the master-craftsmen and builders of the Church.
And the virgins who give praise are those who kept their virginity in holiness and offered praise to God.
"In the church bless God and the Lord from the fountains of Israel."
After this he sets aside the temple of the Jews and brings the Church forward into the midst, and in it he commands all to bless God and the Lord from the fountains of Israel.
That is, the Israelite prophets, who by the grace of the Holy Spirit sprang up like fountains, and prophesied, and taught us men the commandment of God.
We have learned the commandments from the prophets, and we sing to God. "There is Benjamin the young man, astonished [?]" and hastening.
But Aquila says: "Benjamin the young man, mighty"; Theodotion: "Benjamin the young man, untaught and drawing [others]."
For the blessed Paul was of the tribe of Benjamin; from his youth he became a teacher of those set in authority, one who astonished them.
He brought this man, and he was a chosen vessel. And as [?] he was brought up in learning.
"The princes of Judah, their leaders, the princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali."
He has mentioned the kindred of the apostles, tribe by tribe, and the one he calls the brother of the Lord: James, who was the first bishop in Jerusalem, of the tribe of Judah;
Peter and Andrew, James and John and Philip were from the village of Bethsaida; Matthew and James the son of Alphaeus were from Capernaum.
All these were from Galilee, of the tribe of Zebulun and Naphtali.
With the testimony of the prophets and of the Gospel he prophesies this to us and says:
"Of Zebulun and of Naphtali," and the Evangelist says: "The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali.
And the people who sat in darkness, and beyond the Jordan, and Galilee of the Gentiles, who sat in darkness and in the shadows of death, saw a great light."
"Command, O God, by your power, and strengthen this, this which you have established for us from your holy temple, Jerusalem."
And establish this and strengthen us, who from your holy temple, Jerusalem, prophesied concerning the incarnation of your only-begotten Word,
who was exalted to heaven and received worship from all who glorify you, not only at this time
alone, but also in the time to come. According to the saying of Paul, he gave the name Jerusalem to the assembly of the firstborn in heaven.
"To you shall kings offer gifts": the time at which kings would offer worship and gifts, this he had first seen with the prophetic eye and set down as a sign.
"Rebuke the beasts of the reed," and again he says: "Rebuke the beasts of the thicket."
For the thicket and the reed signify barrenness and darkness, into which beasts go to lie in ambush,
but when the love of God for humankind saved us, he rebuked those beasts and drove them away from us.
"The assembly of bullocks among the heifers." Here he calls "bullocks" the leaders of the Jews and their multitude, who became zealous against our Savior.
By the "assembly of heifers" he represents their proud and wanton and [?]-loving women, for another prophet too has many times called that [?] heifers.
"Let those who were tested with silver be turned aside," for they gathered and took counsel, and the betrayers were tested with silver; the evil deed was accomplished,
after which, a short time later, those betrayers were turned back and fell away from their own deeds. But some interpreters said that the testing with silver refers to the saints and the believers,
whereas I have reckoned it, fittingly, as referring to those betrayers, as will those who study with good love, for these verses, taken together, are spoken about their enemies.
"And scatter the nations who desire war": these are the ones who became betrayers, or who became opponents and spoke against God.
Now they have left off the mention of the lawless, and he begins to speak about those who love God. "Apostles came from Egypt, and Ethiopia hastened to give its hand to the Lord."
The Acts of the Apostles bears witness to this, namely what Philip did with the Ethiopian eunuch, who belonged to Queen Candace.
"Kings of the earth, bless God and sing praise to the Lord."

He declares this: that all you impassable and pathless ends [of the earth], receive the light of the worship of the beneficent God, and offer him glory and blessing; make way for him "who sat upon the heaven of heavens from the east."
For as for our Lord Jesus Christ, his appearing in the heavens was not this alone,
but that he had this before, and he sat at the right hand in glory on high, and bestowed on all the shining light of the knowledge of God, and that he was Lord from the setting of the sun,
and truly illumined the darkness, and from the east too he filled all the ends [of the earth].
"Behold, he gave his voice, the voice of power": after the ascension of the Lord, who bestowed the Spirit and made them apostles.
For this reason the Lord says to them, "Sit and wait in this city until you receive power."
Luke teaches us about the voice of power from on high and says, "And there was a voice from heaven," he says, like the sound of many winds, and the house in which the apostles were was filled.
"Give glory to God." The apostle Paul says this: Glorify God with that body of yours.
It is fitting and right, for such great benefits of God our Creator, to give glory to him.
"Over Israel his beauty is great, and his power reaches up to the clouds of heaven," for the apostles were from Israel, through whom he performed very great miracles over all the world.
Just as clouds take up water from the sea and pour down rain unfailingly over all the world,
so too the apostles, who by the grace of the Holy Spirit showed God's love for humankind to all the ends of the earth.
"God is wonderful among his saints." The Lord explained this in the Gospel and says:
"Shed your light upon people, so that they may see your good works and glorify the Father," who art in heaven.
"The God of Israel, he will give power and strength to his people." Baruch mentioned Israel and strength, for as the hope of the fathers and the hymn [?].
And he put away from himself vain strength and firmly accepted Israel; in this same way it came about between the congregation of the old people and that of the new. Blessed be God!
How beautifully the end of the psalm has been brought to completion, for it says: He who has graciously bestowed so many benefits on the human race,

who showed his indescribable and incomprehensible love for humankind and brought about salvation for all the ends of the earth, God Most High is rightly and worthily to be praised, glorified and blessed. Amen.
Glory to you, Christ! The Commentary on the Psalms, spoken by Saint Epiphanius, is finished.
